questions.stem: You need Claude to write a client-facing email about a delayed shipment. Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable first draft?

options.text: 'Give me ideas.'
'Write a client-facing email about a delayed shipment.'
'Write something good about this.'

'You are an operations coordinator. Write a client-facing email about a delayed shipment. Here is the relevant background: [context]. Keep it under 150 words, use a professional but warm tone, and format it as [specific format].'

questions.explanation: The strongest prompt supplies role, context, the concrete task, constraints (length, tone), and the desired output format — the five building blocks that remove guesswork.

questions.stem: You need Claude to write a summary of a competitor's pricing page for the sales team. Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable first draft?

options.text: 'Write something good about this.'
'Give me ideas.'
'Write a summary of a competitor's pricing page for the sales team.'

'You are a sales analyst. Write a summary of a competitor's pricing page for the sales team. Here is the relevant background: [context]. Keep it under 150 words, use a professional but warm tone, and format it as [specific format].'

questions.explanation: The strongest prompt supplies role, context, the concrete task, constraints (length, tone), and the desired output format — the five building blocks that remove guesswork.

questions.stem: You need Claude to write talking points for a town-hall meeting. Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable first draft?

options.text: 'Write talking points for a town-hall meeting.'

'You are an internal communications lead. Write talking points for a town-hall meeting. Here is the relevant background: [context]. Keep it under 150 words, use a professional but warm tone, and format it as [specific format].'
'Write something good about this.'
'Give me ideas.'

questions.explanation: The strongest prompt supplies role, context, the concrete task, constraints (length, tone), and the desired output format — the five building blocks that remove guesswork.

questions.stem: You need Claude to write a first draft of a project status update. Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable first draft?

options.text: 'Write a first draft of a project status update.'

'You are a project manager. Write a first draft of a project status update. Here is the relevant background: [context]. Keep it under 150 words, use a professional but warm tone, and format it as [specific format].'
'Write something good about this.'
'Give me ideas.'

questions.explanation: The strongest prompt supplies role, context, the concrete task, constraints (length, tone), and the desired output format — the five building blocks that remove guesswork.

questions.stem: You need Claude to write a training outline for new hires. Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable first draft?

options.text: 'Give me ideas.'
'Write something good about this.'

'You are an L&D specialist. Write a training outline for new hires. Here is the relevant background: [context]. Keep it under 150 words, use a professional but warm tone, and format it as [specific format].'
'Write a training outline for new hires.'

questions.explanation: The strongest prompt supplies role, context, the concrete task, constraints (length, tone), and the desired output format — the five building blocks that remove guesswork.

questions.stem: You need Claude to write a social post announcing a product update. Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable first draft?

options.text: 'Write a social post announcing a product update.'
'Give me ideas.'
'Write something good about this.'

'You are a marketing associate. Write a social post announcing a product update. Here is the relevant background: [context]. Keep it under 150 words, use a professional but warm tone, and format it as [specific format].'

questions.explanation: The strongest prompt supplies role, context, the concrete task, constraints (length, tone), and the desired output format — the five building blocks that remove guesswork.

questions.stem: Which five elements are commonly identified as the building blocks of an effective business prompt?

options.text: Greeting, body, signature, subject line, attachment
Role, context, task, constraint, format
Model name, temperature, max tokens, system prompt, API key
Grammar, spelling, punctuation, length, font

questions.explanation: Role, context, task, constraint, and format are the standard building blocks taught for effective business prompting.

questions.stem: A prompt says only: 'Write a report.' What is the most likely problem with this prompt?

options.text: There is no problem; short prompts always work best
It is too long
It omits nearly all the building blocks — no context, no specific task detail, no constraints, no format — so Claude has to guess at what's actually needed
It uses too many technical terms

questions.explanation: Missing context, specifics, constraints, and format forces guesswork and produces a generic, likely unusable result.

questions.stem: Which addition would most improve the prompt 'Summarize this document' for a business user who needs it for a specific purpose?

options.text: Adding more punctuation
Nothing; the prompt is already complete
Specifying the audience, desired length, and what the summary will be used for (e.g., 'for an executive who needs 3 bullet points to decide whether to approve the budget')
Removing the word 'document'

questions.explanation: Clarifying audience, length, and purpose turns a vague request into one Claude can target precisely.

questions.stem: In prompt design, what does the 'constraint' building block typically refer to?

options.text: The model's maximum context window size
A password required to access Claude
The number of people who can view the output
Limits the user sets on the output, such as length, tone, or things to avoid

questions.explanation: Constraints are user-specified limits — length, tone, style, things to include or avoid — that shape the output.

questions.stem: A user wants a prompt that reliably produces output formatted as a numbered list of action items with owners and due dates. What should the prompt explicitly specify?

options.text: Nothing beyond the topic; Claude will always guess the right format
The exact output format wanted (numbered list, with owner and due date fields for each item)
Only the tone
Only the audience

questions.explanation: Specifying the exact output format is the most direct way to reliably get a structured list rather than free-flowing prose.

questions.stem: Which prompt best supplies a clear 'role' for Claude to adopt?

options.text: 'Marketing is important.'
'Tell me about ads.'
'As an experienced brand strategist, review this ad copy and suggest three improvements for tone consistency.'
'Write about marketing.'

questions.explanation: Explicitly assigning a role focuses the perspective and expertise Claude brings to the task.

questions.stem: Why does providing context matter when prompting Claude for a business task?

options.text: Context gives Claude the background information it needs to tailor a relevant, accurate response instead of a generic one
Context is only useful for coding tasks
It doesn't matter; Claude already knows all company-specific details
Providing context always makes responses slower with no benefit

questions.explanation: Claude has no independent knowledge of your specific business situation — context supplies exactly what's needed to tailor the response.

questions.stem: A user asks Claude to 'write a project update' without further detail, gets a generic response, and is unsatisfied. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: Project updates cannot be written by AI
The user should have used a different AI product entirely
Claude is malfunctioning
The prompt lacked context, task specifics, constraints, and format guidance, leaving Claude to guess at what a 'good' update looks like

questions.explanation: A generic prompt without the building blocks predictably yields a generic response — this is a prompting issue, not a tool failure.

questions.stem: Which of the following prompts best demonstrates all five building blocks together?

options.text: 'Write an email.'
'Make this better.'
'Reply to this.'

'As our customer support lead, write a reply to the attached complaint about a late delivery. The customer is a long-time client. Keep it empathetic and under 120 words, formatted as a ready-to-send email with a greeting and signature.'

questions.explanation: This prompt specifies role, context, task, constraint, and format all together.

questions.stem: What risk does omitting the 'format' building block create, even when role, context, and task are all well specified?

options.text: No risk; format never matters if the content is good
Omitting format always causes the request to be rejected
Claude may return the right content in a format that doesn't fit how the output will actually be used, requiring rework
Format only matters for coding tasks

questions.explanation: Even excellent content can require rework if it arrives in the wrong shape for its intended use.

questions.stem: A marketing associate needs a prompt for turning bullet-point notes into a polished LinkedIn post. Which detail is LEAST important to include?

options.text: The core message or notes to turn into the post
A rough character/length limit matching LinkedIn norms
The target audience and desired tone
The exact font the final post should display in

questions.explanation: Font is a rendering detail outside Claude's control for a text response; audience, tone, length, and source content actually shape a useful draft.

questions.stem: Why is breaking a large, complex request into smaller steps generally more effective than asking for everything at once?

options.text: It never actually helps; one large prompt is always equivalent
Smaller steps let you review and correct each stage before building on it, reducing the chance an early misunderstanding propagates through the final output
Breaking tasks into steps only matters for coding
It exists purely to increase token usage

questions.explanation: Reviewing intermediate steps catches misunderstandings early, before they compound into a flawed final deliverable.

questions.stem: A user needs a full market-entry analysis covering competitors, pricing, and a go/no-go recommendation. What is a better approach than one giant prompt?

options.text: Ask for the entire analysis in one shot and hope it's coherent
Break it into stages — competitor research, then pricing analysis, then synthesize into a recommendation — reviewing each stage before moving on
There is no better approach; decomposition doesn't help with analysis tasks
Ask Claude to guess which parts matter most and skip the rest

questions.explanation: Staged decomposition lets you validate each component before the final synthesis depends on it.

questions.stem: Which task is the best candidate for decomposition into multiple smaller prompts?

options.text: Fixing a single typo in a sentence
Asking for a one-word yes/no answer
Asking for today's date
Producing a 40-page vendor evaluation report covering multiple vendors, criteria, and a final recommendation

questions.explanation: Large, multi-part deliverables with dependent stages benefit most from decomposition.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to decompose the task 'create a full onboarding plan for new hires'?

options.text: Ask a completely unrelated question first
Ask for the entire plan in a single unstructured request
Decomposition is unnecessary for planning tasks
First outline the key phases, then develop each phase's content in turn, reviewing as you go

questions.explanation: Outlining phases first, then filling in each phase, is a natural staged decomposition that keeps each step reviewable.

questions.stem: After asking Claude to outline a report's structure, what is the most effective next step before requesting the full draft?

options.text: Ask an unrelated question to test Claude's general knowledge
Immediately ask for the full draft with no review of the outline
Start over from scratch with an unrelated prompt
Review and adjust the outline so the foundation is right before the larger draft is built on top of it

questions.explanation: Validating the outline before drafting prevents structural problems from propagating into a much larger piece of work.

questions.stem: What is a key risk of NOT decomposing a very large, multi-part request?

options.text: Large requests are processed identically regardless of decomposition
There is no risk; large single requests always work equally well
A single misunderstanding early in a long response can propagate through the rest of the output, and errors may be harder to spot
Decomposition always produces worse results than one large prompt

questions.explanation: Errors are easier to catch and fix when surfaced at each stage rather than buried inside one long, undifferentiated response.

questions.stem: A user wants Claude to research a topic, draft an article, and then format it for a newsletter. What is a sound decomposition of this request?

options.text: Separate steps: gather the research, then draft the article from that material, then reformat the approved draft for the newsletter
Skip research and go straight to formatting
Ask for the newsletter format before any content exists
One single prompt combining research, drafting, and formatting instructions with no intermediate checkpoints

questions.explanation: Sequencing research, then drafting, then formatting lets each stage build on a validated version of the previous one.

questions.stem: A user decomposes a task into five sequential prompts but doesn't review any intermediate output before issuing the next prompt. What have they lost, compared to true staged decomposition?

options.text: Sequential prompting without review is always faster and equally reliable
Nothing; issuing the prompts in sequence is sufficient regardless of review
The main benefit of decomposition — catching and correcting errors at each stage before they propagate
This approach guarantees a better result than a single combined prompt

questions.explanation: Decomposition's value comes specifically from the review-and-correct opportunity between steps; skipping review forfeits that benefit.

questions.stem: Which best describes when task decomposition is LEAST necessary?

options.text: For a short, simple, single-part request with a clear, low-stakes answer
For a lengthy, multi-stage deliverable with dependencies between sections
For any request involving more than one sentence
Decomposition is always necessary regardless of task size

questions.explanation: Simple, low-stakes, single-part requests don't have the dependency chains that make decomposition valuable.

questions.stem: A user asks for a 'complete competitive analysis, financial model, and go-to-market plan' in one prompt. What is a likely downside of this all-at-once approach?

options.text: Quality across all three deliverables may suffer, and errors in one section are harder to isolate and fix without affecting the others
Combining requests always improves coherence with no downside
No downside; combining unrelated deliverables into one prompt is always optimal
This approach is guaranteed to be faster with no quality tradeoff

questions.explanation: Bundling several substantial, loosely related deliverables into one request makes it harder to isolate and fix problems in any single component.

questions.stem: When a first response from Claude falls short, what is generally the most effective next step?

options.text: Give up on the task entirely
Diagnose specifically what's missing or wrong, then give a targeted follow-up instruction addressing that specific gap
Repeat the identical prompt verbatim and hope for a different result
Switch to writing the entire deliverable by hand with no further use of Claude

questions.explanation: Specific, targeted feedback about what's actually wrong is far more effective than vague dissatisfaction or blind repetition.

questions.stem: A user receives a draft that is 'too long and too formal.' Which follow-up is most likely to produce an improved result?

options.text: 'This is bad, try again.'
'Cut this to about half the length and make the tone more conversational — imagine explaining it to a colleague over coffee.'
Simply resend the exact same original prompt
'Fix it.'

questions.explanation: Naming the specific problems and the specific desired direction gives Claude concrete, actionable feedback.

questions.stem: What is the value of a structured diagnosis (what's wrong, why, what specific change would fix it) before giving feedback to Claude?

options.text: It only helps with coding tasks
It has no value; any vague feedback works equally well
It turns a vague reaction into an actionable instruction Claude can act on directly, rather than leaving Claude to guess what changed
It guarantees a perfect result on the very next attempt

questions.explanation: Concrete, diagnosed feedback removes the guesswork that vague dissatisfaction leaves for the next attempt.

questions.stem: A response nails the content but uses jargon the intended audience won't understand. What is the most precise refinement instruction?

options.text: 'Make it better.'
'This is wrong.'
'Rewrite this for someone with no background in the subject — replace technical terms with plain-language explanations.'
Resend the exact same prompt

questions.explanation: Naming the specific issue and the specific fix is the actionable refinement.

questions.stem: Which feedback is an example of vague, low-value feedback that Claude cannot act on precisely?

options.text: 'This isn't quite right.'
'The second paragraph repeats the first point — please remove the repetition.'
'Replace the word "leverage" with "use" throughout.'
'Shorten the introduction to two sentences.'

questions.explanation: 'This isn't quite right' gives no specific, actionable direction, unlike the other options.

questions.stem: Why is reissuing the exact same prompt after an unsatisfactory response usually ineffective?

options.text: It is always effective and guaranteed to fix the issue
Resending prompts is technically impossible
Claude only allows a prompt to be sent once
Without new information about what specifically needs to change, there's little reason to expect a meaningfully different or better result

questions.explanation: Without added or corrected information, there's no new signal to change the outcome meaningfully.

questions.stem: A user isn't sure exactly what's wrong with a response, only that 'something feels off.' What is a productive way to proceed?

options.text: Ask Claude to explain its reasoning or assumptions for the parts that feel off, which can surface the specific issue and inform a targeted fix
Repeat the same prompt with no changes
Give up and write the whole thing manually
Assume the response is fine despite the discomfort

questions.explanation: Prompting Claude to surface its reasoning/assumptions can help pinpoint vague discomfort into something specific and fixable.

questions.stem: A draft correctly follows every instruction given, but the user is unsatisfied because an important requirement was never actually stated. What is the real issue here?

options.text: The original prompt was incomplete — the missing requirement needs to be added explicitly in a follow-up
Claude made an error that needs correcting
The user should abandon the task
This situation is impossible

questions.explanation: If an unstated requirement wasn't met, that's a prompting gap to fill in, not necessarily a model mistake.

questions.stem: What is the benefit of iterating in small, targeted steps versus bundling many unrelated changes into one revision request?

options.text: Bundling changes is always faster with no tradeoff
Targeted iteration is only relevant for coding tasks
It's easier to verify each specific change worked, and to isolate the source if the revision introduces a new problem
There is no benefit; bundling is always equally effective

questions.explanation: Isolating changes makes it easier to confirm each fix worked and trace any new issue back to its source.

questions.stem: After three rounds of revision, a draft still misses the mark in the same way each time. What does this suggest?

options.text: Nothing; this is expected and unrelated to feedback quality
Claude is incapable of ever producing a correct response
The task should be abandoned permanently
The feedback given may not be specifically targeting the actual root issue, and it's worth re-diagnosing the problem more precisely

questions.explanation: A repeated, unresolved issue across multiple rounds signals a need to re-diagnose the actual root cause.

questions.stem: For a brainstorming task where the goal is a wide variety of creative ideas, which prompting approach is most effective?

options.text: Ask for exactly one 'correct' idea and stop
Avoid giving any topic at all
Constrain the response to a single rigid format with no room for variation
Explicitly ask for a large number of diverse ideas, encourage unconventional options, and defer judging quality until after generation

questions.explanation: Brainstorming benefits from explicitly requesting volume and diversity, and separating idea generation from evaluation.

questions.stem: For a research-summary task, which detail is most important to include in the prompt?

options.text: The user's favorite color
What sources or materials to draw from, and what specific questions the summary needs to answer
The exact time of day the request was made
Nothing beyond the topic name

questions.explanation: Specifying source material and the specific questions to answer focuses a research summary on what's actually needed.

questions.stem: For a drafting task (e.g., writing a formal proposal), which prompting detail matters most beyond the core content?

options.text: Audience, tone, and structural conventions expected for that document type
The exact number of times the word 'the' should appear
Nothing; drafting tasks need no additional detail beyond the topic
The user's internal task-tracking ID

questions.explanation: Audience, tone, and structural/genre conventions most directly shape whether a draft reads appropriately for its purpose.

questions.stem: A user needs Claude to analyze a dataset summary and identify trends. Which prompting element is most critical?

options.text: A request for creative flourishes and metaphors
Clarity about which specific questions or comparisons the analysis should address
No specifics at all beyond 'analyze this'
A request for the longest possible response

questions.explanation: Analytical tasks benefit from specific, targeted questions rather than an open-ended 'analyze this' with no direction.

questions.stem: Why might the same prompting principles need to be applied differently for a brainstorming task versus a drafting task?

options.text: They don't need to be applied differently at all
Brainstorming benefits from loosening constraints to encourage volume/variety, while drafting benefits from tighter constraints to produce a usable, polished result
Brainstorming should always have the strictest constraints of any task type
Task type has no bearing on how constraints should be set

questions.explanation: The right balance of constraint vs. openness shifts with the task's goal.

questions.stem: A user brainstorming names for a new product gets ten very similar, safe suggestions. What prompt adjustment would likely produce more variety?

options.text: Ask for the exact same prompt again with no changes
Explicitly ask for a wider range, including some bold or unconventional options, grouped by different themes or angles
Reduce the number of ideas requested
Remove all context about the product

questions.explanation: Directly asking for range, unconventional options, or varied angles counteracts a tendency toward safe, similar suggestions.

questions.stem: For a research task requiring up-to-date facts, which caveat is most important for the user to keep in mind?

options.text: None; all information Claude provides is always guaranteed current and correct
Claude's knowledge may not reflect the most recent developments unless using a feature designed for current information, so time-sensitive facts should be verified
Research tasks should never be attempted with AI assistance
Research tasks require no verification of any kind

questions.explanation: Recognizing the limits of static knowledge and verifying time-sensitive claims is central to responsible research use.

questions.stem: Which is the best prompting approach for drafting a formal client-facing letter versus an internal quick-note?

options.text: Specify a more formal tone and careful structure for the client letter, while allowing a more casual, abbreviated style for the internal note
Always default to the most formal tone regardless of audience
Always default to the most casual tone regardless of audience
Use identical instructions for both; formality never needs to be specified

questions.explanation: Matching tone and structure to the audience and stakes of each document type is a core task-type prompting adjustment.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an 'analysis' task from a 'drafting' task in terms of prompting needs?

options.text: Drafting tasks never need any context
There is no meaningful distinction
Analysis tasks need clear evaluative questions/criteria; drafting tasks need clear tone, structure, and audience guidance
Analysis tasks never need any context

questions.explanation: Each task type has different success criteria, shifting the prompting emphasis accordingly.

questions.stem: A user wants both a brainstorm of options AND a recommendation of the best one. What is a sound way to structure this request?

options.text: Skip the brainstorm entirely and ask only for one final answer
There is no reasonable way to combine these two goals
First request a wide brainstorm without judgment, then in a follow-up ask Claude to evaluate the list and recommend the strongest option against stated criteria
Ask for both simultaneously with no separation, and hope the two goals don't interfere

questions.explanation: Separating divergent brainstorming from convergent evaluation avoids one goal narrowing the other prematurely.

questions.stem: Which is a reasonable adaptation when a research summary needs to serve a non-expert executive audience rather than a technical team?

options.text: Emphasize implications and recommendations over technical detail, and define or avoid jargon the executive audience won't need
Make the summary as long as possible regardless of audience
Add more technical jargon to seem more credible
No adaptation needed; the same summary works for every audience

questions.explanation: Tailoring depth, jargon, and emphasis to the audience's needs is central to adapting a summary for a different reader.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to explicitly tell Claude which task type you're aiming for (e.g., 'this is a brainstorm, not a final decision')?

options.text: It isn't useful; task type has no bearing on the response
It helps calibrate the response's tone and scope — generating many loose ideas versus committing to one polished, final answer
It only matters for very long documents
Task type framing is only relevant in coding contexts

questions.explanation: Naming the task type helps Claude calibrate whether to prioritize breadth/creativity or precision/finality.

questions.stem: A user consistently gets safe, predictable brainstorm results. Which prompt change is most likely to increase variety?

options.text: Removing all context about the goal
Asking for only one idea at a time
Explicitly inviting unconventional, even impractical ideas as part of the initial brainstorm, before filtering for feasibility later
Requesting the shortest possible response

questions.explanation: Explicitly inviting unconventional ideas up front, with feasibility filtering deferred, tends to widen the range generated.

questions.stem: Why might separating 'idea generation' from 'idea evaluation' into two distinct steps improve brainstorming quality?

options.text: It doesn't; combining them is always better
Evaluating too early can suppress unconventional but potentially valuable ideas before they're even fully generated
Separating the steps always doubles the cost with no benefit
This separation only matters for coding tasks

questions.explanation: Premature judgment during generation can filter out ideas that seem odd at first but have real value.

questions.stem: Which prompt is more likely to produce genuinely varied brainstorm output?

options.text: 'Give me 5 marketing slogans.'
'Give me 15 marketing slogans spanning different tones — playful, serious, minimalist, bold — and don't filter for quality yet.'
'Give me the best marketing slogan.'
'Give me a marketing slogan like the last one.'

questions.explanation: Requesting more ideas across explicitly different tones, with quality filtering deferred, maximizes variety.

questions.stem: A brainstorm session keeps returning ideas similar to a previous, already-rejected suggestion. What is a useful next prompt?

options.text: Explicitly state which direction was already rejected and ask for ideas that deliberately avoid that direction
Give up on brainstorming entirely
Repeat the identical brainstorm prompt again
Ask for exactly the same idea restated in different words

questions.explanation: Explicitly ruling out the already-rejected direction gives Claude a concrete constraint that pushes toward new territory.

questions.stem: What role can asking Claude to 'think like' a specific persona (e.g., a skeptical customer) play in creative tasks?

options.text: No role; personas never affect output
It can surface a different angle or set of concerns than a neutral, generic response would, adding variety and perspective
Personas can only be used for customer service tasks
Personas guarantee factual accuracy

questions.explanation: Persona framing is a lightweight way to inject a different perspective and widen the range of ideas generated.

questions.stem: Which instruction is most likely to help if brainstormed options all feel formulaic and interchangeable?

options.text: Ask for the ideas to be shortened
Repeat the original prompt with no changes
Ask for fewer ideas overall
Ask Claude to approach the problem from several explicitly different angles rather than one general framing

questions.explanation: Explicitly varying the framing/angle for each batch of ideas breaks out of formulaic, interchangeable output.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to explicitly permit 'impractical' ideas during an early brainstorming pass?

options.text: Impractical ideas are always the best ones
Allowing impractical ideas widens the exploration space, and a seemingly impractical idea can sometimes be refined into a valuable one during later filtering
This has no effect on the range of ideas generated
It guarantees higher-quality output with no filtering needed

questions.explanation: Widening the net during generation and filtering later increases the odds of finding valuable ideas a narrower framing would exclude.

questions.stem: A team needs fresh angles on a stale internal process. Which prompting technique best supports this goal?

options.text: Avoid mentioning the current process at all
Ask for the shortest possible answer with no elaboration
Ask only for minor wording tweaks to the existing process description
Ask Claude to reimagine the process from scratch with a stated goal, then compare to the current approach

questions.explanation: A 'reimagine from scratch' framing removes the anchoring effect of the existing process, surfacing more genuinely fresh ideas.

questions.stem: A user wants Claude to match a specific writing style used in past company communications. What is the most effective way to convey this?

options.text: Avoid giving any guidance and hope for the best
Assume Claude already knows the company's style without any input
Provide one or two representative examples of the desired style alongside a description of what makes them effective
Describe the style in abstract terms only, with no example

questions.explanation: Concrete examples anchor abstract style descriptions and give Claude something specific to match.

questions.stem: Why can providing an example of the desired output format improve reliability for a recurring business task?

options.text: Examples never help; only written instructions matter
A concrete example resolves ambiguity that a purely descriptive instruction might leave open
Examples only work for creative writing tasks
Providing examples always makes responses less accurate

questions.explanation: A concrete example removes ambiguity a written description alone might leave, improving consistency.

questions.stem: A user provides one example of a well-written meeting summary and asks Claude to write a new one in the same style. What is this technique called?

options.text: Zero-shot prompting
Example-driven (few-shot) prompting
Prompt injection
Extended thinking

questions.explanation: Providing one or more examples to guide style/format is example-driven, or 'few-shot,' prompting.

questions.stem: Which is a risk of providing only ONE example when asking Claude to match a style?

options.text: There is no risk; one example is always sufficient
Providing examples is never appropriate in business contexts
One example always produces worse results than zero examples
Claude might over-fit to incidental details of that single example rather than the general stylistic pattern intended

questions.explanation: A single example risks the model picking up incidental specifics rather than the general pattern.

questions.stem: What should a good example for style-matching typically demonstrate?

options.text: An example is only useful if it's on the exact same topic as the new request
Only the topic, with no attention to tone or structure
The tone, structure, and level of formality/detail that should be replicated in the new output
Examples should be as long and detailed as possible regardless of relevance

questions.explanation: A useful example demonstrates transferable qualities rather than requiring an identical topic.

questions.stem: A user wants consistent formatting across many similar weekly reports. What is an efficient way to achieve this using examples?

options.text: Write a brand-new set of instructions from scratch every week
Save a well-formatted past report as a reference example and provide it each time a new report is requested
Avoid using any consistent format at all
Ask for a different format every week to keep things fresh

questions.explanation: Reusing a validated example as a template efficiently maintains consistency across recurring deliverables.

questions.stem: Why might describing a desired tone in words ('professional but warm') sometimes be less effective than showing an example of that tone?

options.text: Tone can be subjective and open to interpretation in words alone; a concrete example removes ambiguity about what's intended
Examples are only useful for grammar correction
Word descriptions are always more effective than examples
There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches

questions.explanation: Abstract tone descriptions can be interpreted several ways; a concrete example pins down exactly what's intended.

questions.stem: Which scenario is the best candidate for using an example-driven prompt?

options.text: A request for Claude's general opinion on an unrelated topic
A simple factual question with a single correct answer
A recurring task (like weekly reports) where past well-received outputs exist as reference material
A completely novel, one-off request with no precedent or reference material

questions.explanation: Recurring tasks with existing reference material are exactly where example-driven prompting adds the most consistency value.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to use an example that is a close but imperfect match to the current task?

options.text: Assume Claude will ignore the example automatically
Provide it with no context about how it should or shouldn't be used
Discard the example entirely since it isn't a perfect match
Provide it while explicitly noting which aspects to follow and which don't apply to the current task

questions.explanation: Explicitly framing which parts of an imperfect example are relevant avoids over-generalizing from irrelevant specifics.

questions.stem: Why should a prompt for a business deliverable typically specify a target length?

options.text: Length is irrelevant to how useful a response is
Without a length target, Claude may produce something far too long or too short for its intended use, requiring rework
Specifying length always reduces the quality of the content
Length can never be controlled through prompting

questions.explanation: An unspecified length leaves Claude guessing, which risks a mismatch with what's actually usable.

questions.stem: A user needs output formatted as a table with three columns: Task, Owner, Deadline. What should the prompt include?

options.text: No formatting guidance; Claude will always default to the requested table
An explicit request for a table with those three specific column headers
A request for a paragraph instead, since tables aren't supported
A request to avoid using any structure at all

questions.explanation: Explicitly naming the desired structure and column headers is the most direct way to reliably get that exact format.

questions.stem: A user gets a well-written but overly long response for a task that needed a quick two-sentence answer. What prompting change would prevent this next time?

options.text: Avoid using Claude for short answers in the future
Nothing can be done; length cannot be controlled
Explicitly state the desired length constraint up front (e.g., 'answer in two sentences or fewer')
Ask an unrelated follow-up question

questions.explanation: Stating the length constraint directly in the prompt is the most reliable way to get a concise response the first time.

questions.stem: Which format specification is most useful when the output needs to be pasted directly into a specific downstream tool?

options.text: A request for the longest possible response regardless of destination
No format specification is ever necessary
A request to avoid any structure whatsoever
Naming the destination and its formatting conventions (e.g., comma-separated values for a spreadsheet, short bullets for a slide)

questions.explanation: Naming the destination and its conventions gives Claude the concrete target format needed for smooth downstream use.

questions.stem: Which prompt best specifies both format and length together?

options.text: 'Summarize the quarterly results in exactly 3 bullet points, each one sentence long.'
'Results?'
'Tell me about the quarterly results.'
'Write something about the results.'

questions.explanation: This prompt specifies structure (bullet points), count (3), and length per point (one sentence).

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to request output that will be read on a mobile device with limited screen space?

options.text: Ask for shorter paragraphs, more white space, and perhaps bullet points rather than dense blocks of text
No adjustment is needed regardless of the reading device
Ask for the longest, most detailed response possible
Ask Claude to ignore formatting entirely

questions.explanation: Adapting format to the reading context improves usability on constrained screens.

questions.stem: A recurring weekly report needs the exact same section headers every time. What is the most reliable way to enforce this via prompting?

options.text: Rely on Claude to remember the headers from a previous, separate conversation automatically
Explicitly list the exact section headers required in each new prompt, or persist them via a saved Project instruction
Never specify headers and accept whatever structure comes back
Ask for a completely different structure each week

questions.explanation: Explicitly restating or persisting the exact required headers is the reliable way to enforce consistent structure.

questions.stem: Why might requesting 'no more than 5 bullet points' be more useful than simply saying 'be concise'?

options.text: 'Be concise' always produces shorter output than a specific count
There is no meaningful difference between the two instructions
Specific counts are impossible for Claude to follow
A specific, measurable constraint is less open to interpretation than a subjective term like 'concise'

questions.explanation: Concrete, measurable constraints reduce ambiguity compared to subjective terms, improving reliability of the result.

questions.stem: A user wants a response broken into clearly labeled sections (Background, Analysis, Recommendation). What is the best way to ensure this structure?

options.text: Ask for a single unstructured paragraph
Provide the labels only after receiving the response, as a correction
Say nothing about structure and hope Claude infers it
Explicitly request those three labeled sections, in that order, in the prompt

questions.explanation: Explicitly requesting the exact labeled sections up front is more direct than correcting after the fact.

questions.stem: What is a 'hallucination' in the context of AI-generated content?

options.text: A deliberate lie the model tells to deceive the user
Confidently stated, fluent-sounding content that is factually incorrect or fabricated, without any signal that it might be wrong
A visual glitch in the user interface
Any response the user personally disagrees with

questions.explanation: A hallucination is fabricated or incorrect content stated with the same fluent confidence as accurate content, with no built-in warning sign.

questions.stem: Claude's response includes a specific statistic ('42% of surveyed users preferred Option B') with no source cited. What is the appropriate response from a careful user?

options.text: Ignore the number's specificity as irrelevant to whether it needs checking
Accept the number as accurate since it sounds specific and plausible
Treat specific, uncited numbers as unverified and check them against an actual source before using them in a real deliverable
Assume all numbers Claude produces are automatically sourced and correct

questions.explanation: Specificity makes a fabricated number sound more credible, not more accurate — uncited figures should be verified before use.

questions.stem: Why are hallucinations often described as particularly risky compared to other kinds of errors?

options.text: They are always flagged automatically by the interface
They tend to be stated fluently and confidently, with no stylistic difference from accurate content, making them harder to catch without independent verification
They only ever occur in very short responses
They are impossible to occur in business contexts

questions.explanation: The fluency and confidence of hallucinated content is exactly what makes it dangerous — there's no built-in tell distinguishing it from accurate content.

questions.stem: A response cites a specific case name and year for a legal precedent. What is the appropriate level of trust to place in this citation without further checking?

options.text: Limited trust until verified against a primary legal source, since fabricated but plausible-looking citations are a known risk
No response involving legal topics should ever be reviewed
Full trust; legal citations are always accurate
Trust should scale with how confident the tone of the response sounds

questions.explanation: Fabricated citations that look completely legitimate are a well-documented hallucination pattern, warranting verification against a primary source regardless of tone.

questions.stem: Which of these is a red flag that should prompt extra scrutiny for potential hallucination?

options.text: A response that hedges and says 'I'm not fully certain about this figure'
A response stating a highly specific fact (exact percentage, date, or citation) with no indication of its source
A response that explicitly recommends checking a primary source
A response that declines to answer a question outside its knowledge

questions.explanation: Ironically, unsourced but highly specific claims deserve more scrutiny than appropriately hedged ones, since specificity can create false confidence.

questions.stem: A user asks Claude for 'the exact revenue figures for a private company that doesn't publicly disclose financials.' Which outcome should the user be most alert to?

options.text: This type of question never carries hallucination risk
Claude will always correctly state that the data isn't available
The response will always be flagged automatically as an estimate
Claude might produce a plausible-sounding but fabricated estimate presented as if it were a known fact, since the true figures don't exist in public data

questions.explanation: Asking for specific data that isn't actually available anywhere is a classic setup for a fabricated-sounding, false-confidence answer.

questions.stem: What is the safest general practice for using any specific factual claim from Claude in a high-stakes business deliverable?

options.text: Use it directly with no verification, since Claude is generally reliable
Only verify claims that sound obviously wrong
Verification is unnecessary if the response sounds confident
Verify it against an independent, authoritative source before relying on it in the deliverable

questions.explanation: Independent verification — not the confidence or plausibility of the phrasing — is the reliable safeguard against hallucinated facts.

questions.stem: Which scenario carries the highest hallucination risk for a business user to be alert to?

options.text: Asking Claude to format a list alphabetically
Asking Claude to summarize a document the user has provided in full
Asking Claude for precise, obscure statistics or citations on a narrow topic where verifiable data may be scarce
Asking Claude to rephrase a paragraph the user already wrote

questions.explanation: Requests for precise data in low-availability, narrow domains are where models are most likely to fill gaps with plausible-sounding fabrication.

questions.stem: Why is 'it sounds confident and detailed' NOT a reliable signal that a claim is accurate?

options.text: Confidence and detail always correlate perfectly with accuracy
Detail is always a sign of fabrication, and vagueness is always a sign of accuracy
Fabricated content can be just as fluent, confident, and detailed as accurate content, so tone alone doesn't distinguish the two
This is actually a reliable signal and should be trusted

questions.explanation: Fluency and confidence are stylistic properties, not accuracy signals — hallucinations frequently share both.

questions.stem: A response includes a quote attributed to a named individual. What should a careful user do before using this quote publicly?

options.text: Remove the quotation marks and publish it as a paraphrase with no further check
Assume quotation marks guarantee the text is a verified, real quote
Publish it immediately since it's in quotation marks
Verify the quote's accuracy and attribution against a primary or reliable source before using it, since fabricated quotes are a known risk

questions.explanation: Quotation marks don't guarantee authenticity — attributed quotes should be checked against a real source before public use.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable interpretation if Claude says 'I don't have reliable information on this specific detail'?

options.text: This should be treated as a system malfunction
This is a useful, honest signal that should be respected rather than pushed past by demanding a specific-sounding answer anyway
The user should keep re-asking until a specific answer is produced regardless
This response type never occurs in practice

questions.explanation: An appropriately hedged 'I don't know' is more trustworthy than a fabricated specific answer, and should be respected rather than pressured away.

questions.stem: A financial report draft includes a specific interest rate figure attributed to 'recent market data.' What is the appropriate verification step?

options.text: None; the phrase 'recent market data' is sufficient sourcing
Trace the figure back to an actual, current, named source (e.g., a specific financial data provider or filing) before including it in the final report
Round the number to make it seem less precise and therefore safer
Replace the number with a random alternative

questions.explanation: A vague attribution like 'recent market data' isn't a real source — the figure needs to be traced to something concrete and verifiable.

questions.stem: Which technical parameter, if fabricated in a response, would be especially risky in a safety-relevant business context (e.g., a chemical handling guideline)?

options.text: The document's font size
A stylistic word choice
The order of paragraphs in the response
A specific numeric threshold or specification presented as an established standard

questions.explanation: Fabricated numeric thresholds in safety-relevant contexts carry real-world consequences if acted on without verification.

questions.stem: Which practice most directly reduces the risk of a hallucinated fact making it into a final business deliverable?

options.text: Cross-checking specific factual claims, numbers, and citations against independent, authoritative sources before finalizing
Skimming the response quickly for overall tone
Assuming longer responses are inherently more accurate than shorter ones
Trusting responses that use more technical vocabulary

questions.explanation: Independent cross-checking of specific claims is the direct, reliable mitigation — tone, vocabulary, and length are not accuracy signals.

questions.stem: Why might hallucinations be more likely when asking about very recent events or niche, low-coverage topics?

options.text: Sparse or outdated underlying information increases the chance the model fills gaps with plausible-sounding but unverified content
Hallucination risk is unrelated to topic recency or coverage
Niche topics are always safer because they're 'less popular'
Recent events are always described with an explicit disclaimer

questions.explanation: Where reliable information is thin, there's more room for confident-sounding gap-filling that isn't grounded in fact.

questions.stem: A user notices a response's numbers don't quite add up when checked against each other (e.g., percentages that don't sum correctly). What should this internal inconsistency suggest?

options.text: A signal to scrutinize the entire set of figures more closely, since internal inconsistency is a concrete, checkable sign that something in the response may be unreliable
Nothing; internal math inconsistencies are irrelevant to accuracy
The document should be published immediately without further review
The response should be trusted more, since minor errors indicate careful human-like work

questions.explanation: Internally inconsistent numbers are a concrete, easily checkable red flag worth investigating before the figures are used further.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable relationship between how important a specific fact is to a decision and how much verification effort it deserves?

options.text: All facts deserve identical verification effort regardless of importance
Facts that are more consequential to the decision being made deserve proportionally more verification effort before being relied upon
Less important facts deserve more scrutiny than important ones
Verification effort should be random and unrelated to the fact's importance

questions.explanation: Risk-proportional verification — more scrutiny for higher-stakes claims — is a practical, efficient approach to fact-checking AI output.

questions.stem: A user asks Claude to name the specific page number in a long uploaded document where a claim appears, and Claude provides one. What should the user do before relying on that page number?

options.text: Trust it completely without checking, since Claude had access to the document
Spot-check the cited page to confirm the claim actually appears there, since fabricated or imprecise page references can still occur
Assume the page number is irrelevant to the claim's accuracy
Delete the citation entirely regardless of its accuracy

questions.explanation: Even with document access, spot-checking specific pinpoint citations is a cheap, worthwhile verification step before relying on them.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the core skill this topic is testing?

options.text: Understanding that hallucinations only occur in coding-related responses
Memorizing a list of topics Claude cannot discuss
Knowing how to disable Claude's response generation entirely
Recognizing that fluent, confident-sounding AI output is not the same as verified, accurate output, and knowing when independent verification is warranted

questions.explanation: The central skill is separating the feeling of confidence in a response from its actual, independently verifiable accuracy.

questions.stem: A user is under time pressure and tempted to skip verifying a specific, plausible-sounding statistic in a client-facing report. What is the most responsible course of action?

options.text: Either verify the figure quickly against a real source or clearly flag it as unverified/remove it, rather than presenting an unchecked number as fact under time pressure
Skip verification since the deadline is tight and the number sounds reasonable
Increase the number slightly to make it sound more impressive
Ask a colleague to guess whether the number seems right

questions.explanation: Time pressure doesn't reduce the risk of an unverified figure being wrong — the responsible options are quick verification or explicit flagging/removal, not silent inclusion.

questions.stem: What is a 'primary source' in the context of fact-checking an AI-generated claim?

options.text: The original, authoritative document or dataset where a fact originates (e.g., the actual filing, statute, or dataset), rather than a secondhand summary
The AI model's own explanation of where it got the information
Whichever source agrees with the AI-generated claim
Any website that appears first in a search engine

questions.explanation: A primary source is the original, authoritative origin of a fact, which is what should be checked against, not a secondhand restatement.

questions.stem: A report claims a specific regulation requires a certain action. What is the most reliable way to verify this claim?

options.text: Trust the AI-generated summary as sufficient on its own
Look up the actual regulatory text or an official government source to confirm the requirement as stated
Ask a different AI model the same question and compare tone
Assume regulatory claims never need verification

questions.explanation: Checking the actual regulatory text or an official source is the direct way to confirm a legal/regulatory claim.

questions.stem: A financial figure in a draft is attributed to 'the company's annual report.' What is the appropriate verification step?

options.text: Assume the attribution is accurate without opening the actual report
Change the figure to a rounder number for safety
Remove the attribution entirely and present the figure as general knowledge
Open the actual annual report and confirm the figure appears there as stated

questions.explanation: Directly checking the named source document is the concrete verification step — an attribution alone isn't verification.

questions.stem: Why is checking a secondary summary (e.g., a news article about a report) generally less reliable than checking the primary source directly?

options.text: Secondary summaries are always completely accurate
There is no difference in reliability between primary and secondary sources
Primary sources are always less accurate than secondary summaries
Secondary summaries can introduce their own errors, omissions, or interpretive spin between the primary source and the final claim

questions.explanation: Each layer of summarization is a chance for error or distortion to be introduced, making the primary source the more reliable check.

questions.stem: A technical specification (e.g., a maximum load capacity) appears in a draft with no clear source. What should happen before this spec is used in a real engineering or safety context?

options.text: Publish it as-is since it looks like a normal technical detail
Trace it to an authoritative technical standard or manufacturer specification and confirm it matches exactly before relying on it
Round the number up to be safe
Assume all technical specifications generated by AI are pre-verified

questions.explanation: Safety-relevant technical specifications need to be traced to and confirmed against an authoritative standard, not assumed correct.

questions.stem: What should a user do if a primary source cannot be located to verify a specific claim?

options.text: Publish the claim with extra confidence to compensate
Assume the claim is true since no source contradicts it
Ask Claude to simply repeat the same claim as confirmation
Treat the claim as unverified and either clearly flag it as such or omit it from a deliverable that depends on its accuracy

questions.explanation: Inability to locate a primary source is a reason for caution and flagging, not for treating an unverifiable claim as confirmed.

questions.stem: A user is fact-checking a claim about a specific law's effective date. Which of the following is the strongest source to check?

options.text: A social media post referencing the law
The AI response's own restated confidence level
A general web search result summary with no named source
The official government or legislative record for that law

questions.explanation: The official government/legislative record is the authoritative primary source for a law's effective date.

questions.stem: Why is fact-checking against a primary source especially important for legal citations included in AI-generated content?

options.text: Legal citations are always accurate by default and need no checking
Fabricated but plausible-looking legal citations are a documented risk, and using an unverified citation in a legal or compliance context can have serious consequences
Legal citations never appear in AI-generated content
Checking legal citations is only necessary for criminal cases

questions.explanation: The stakes of an incorrect or fabricated legal citation, combined with the known hallucination risk, make primary-source verification essential here.

questions.stem: A user has both an AI-generated summary and access to the original source document. What is the most reliable verification workflow?

options.text: Spot-check key claims in the summary against the specific relevant passages in the original document
Discard the original document since the summary exists
Rely solely on the AI summary and never open the original
Assume the summary is by definition more accurate than the source

questions.explanation: Spot-checking key claims against the actual source passages is the practical, reliable way to validate a summary.

questions.stem: What distinguishes 'fact-checking' from simply 'reading the response carefully'?

options.text: Fact-checking is only relevant for numerical claims, never textual ones
They are the same activity with no meaningful difference
Fact-checking involves actively comparing specific claims against an independent, authoritative source, not just assessing whether the response reads plausibly
Careful reading is always sufficient and fact-checking is unnecessary

questions.explanation: Careful reading assesses internal plausibility; fact-checking requires an external, independent comparison point.

questions.stem: A user finds that a primary source contradicts a specific claim in Claude's response. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Correct the claim in the deliverable to match the verified primary source
Ignore the contradiction since the AI response sounded confident
Include both contradictory versions with no resolution
Trust the AI-generated claim over the primary source

questions.explanation: When a verified primary source contradicts an AI claim, the primary source should take precedence in the final deliverable.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best example of a primary source for a claim about a company's quarterly revenue?

options.text: The company's own official quarterly financial filing or earnings release
An AI-generated estimate with no cited source
A blog post summarizing 'some recent news about the company'
A rumor shared on an online forum

questions.explanation: The company's own official filing or earnings release is the authoritative primary source for its reported revenue.

questions.stem: A user is preparing a client-facing document citing an industry statistic. What is the strongest verification practice?

options.text: Use the AI-generated statistic as-is, since it sounds authoritative
Locate the original study or dataset behind the statistic and confirm the number and its context (e.g., sample size, year) match what's being claimed
Change the statistic slightly so it can't be checked
Remove all numbers from the document to avoid the issue entirely

questions.explanation: Tracing to the original study/dataset and confirming both the number and its context is the thorough, correct verification approach.

questions.stem: Why might checking 'context' (e.g., sample size, date, scope) matter as much as checking the raw number itself when fact-checking a statistic?

options.text: Numbers are always self-explanatory with no need for context
Context checking is only relevant for scientific papers
Context never matters; only the raw number needs checking
A technically correct number can still be misleading if its context (e.g., a tiny sample size or an outdated date) isn't accurately represented

questions.explanation: A correct number with missing or misrepresented context can still lead to a misleading conclusion, so context is part of a complete fact-check.

questions.stem: A draft states a fact 'according to a well-known study,' with no further detail. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Accept the vague attribution as sufficient sourcing
Ask for or independently find the specific study being referenced, and verify the claim directly against it
Assume 'well-known' means verification is unnecessary
Remove the word 'study' but keep the unverified claim

questions.explanation: A vague attribution like 'a well-known study' isn't a real, checkable source — the specific study needs to be identified and checked directly.

questions.stem: What is a practical benefit of building a habit of checking primary sources for high-stakes claims, even when a claim seems obviously true?

options.text: It catches the occasional subtly wrong or outdated 'obvious' fact before it causes real harm, and reinforces a consistent, disciplined verification habit
There is no benefit; obviously true claims never need checking
It always slows down work with no offsetting benefit
It is only useful for claims that seem obviously false

questions.explanation: Consistent verification habits catch the rare but costly cases where an 'obvious' fact turns out to be subtly wrong or outdated.

questions.stem: A user needs to verify a claim about a competitor's product feature. Which is the strongest source to check?

options.text: An anonymous online comment about the competitor
The competitor's own official product documentation or website
The AI response's own restated confidence
A completely unrelated company's documentation

questions.explanation: The competitor's own official documentation is the authoritative primary source for claims about their product's actual features.

questions.stem: What does evaluating a document's 'internal consistency' mean?

options.text: Checking whether the document uses a consistent font
Checking whether claims, numbers, and conclusions in different parts of the document agree with each other rather than contradicting one another
Checking whether the document was written quickly
Checking whether the document matches a competitor's document

questions.explanation: Internal consistency means the document doesn't contradict itself across its own sections, numbers, or conclusions.

questions.stem: A report's executive summary states a recommendation that isn't actually supported by the analysis in the body of the report. What kind of problem is this?

options.text: A formatting-only issue unrelated to content quality
A minor stylistic issue with no real impact
A structural/logical consistency problem — the conclusion doesn't follow from the presented evidence, and this should be caught before the report is finalized
This is not a real problem worth checking for

questions.explanation: A conclusion unsupported by the body's evidence is a genuine logical-consistency flaw, not a cosmetic issue.

questions.stem: Why is checking a document's overall logical flow important, even if each individual sentence is well-written?

options.text: Logical flow is irrelevant to document quality
Individual sentence quality guarantees the document as a whole makes sense
This only matters for creative writing, not business documents
Well-written individual sentences can still fail to build toward a coherent overall argument or structure if the flow between them isn't checked

questions.explanation: Sentence-level polish doesn't guarantee document-level coherence — the overall argument structure needs separate evaluation.

questions.stem: A proposal recommends 'Option A' in its conclusion but the comparison table earlier in the document shows 'Option B' scoring higher on every criterion. What should a careful reviewer do?

options.text: Ignore the discrepancy since the writing quality is otherwise good
Publish both conflicting conclusions and let the reader decide
Flag the inconsistency and resolve it — either correct the recommendation or correct the comparison table — before finalizing the document
Delete the comparison table to hide the discrepancy

questions.explanation: A direct contradiction between the supporting data and the stated conclusion must be resolved, not published or ignored.

questions.stem: What does 'audience suitability' mean when evaluating a document's structure?

options.text: Whether the document uses the reader's preferred font
Whether the content's depth, tone, and structure are appropriate for who will actually be reading and using the document
Whether the document is the correct file size
Whether the document was proofread for spelling only

questions.explanation: Audience suitability is about matching depth, tone, and structure to the actual reader's needs and expertise level.

questions.stem: A technical document intended for a general business audience is full of unexplained jargon and deep technical detail. What evaluation issue does this represent?

options.text: No issue; more detail is always better regardless of audience
A purely cosmetic issue unrelated to the document's usefulness
This is only a problem if the reader explicitly complains
A mismatch between the document's structure/content and its intended audience, which should be flagged and revised before distribution

questions.explanation: Content that doesn't match the audience's background undermines the document's usefulness, regardless of technical accuracy.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a structural (not factual) problem in a document?

options.text: A statistic that is factually wrong
A conclusion section that doesn't logically follow from the evidence presented earlier in the same document
A citation that cannot be found in any source
A quote that was never actually said

questions.explanation: A conclusion misaligned with its own supporting evidence is a structural/logical flaw, distinct from a factual accuracy error.

questions.stem: A user reviewing a long report notices that terminology for the same concept changes partway through (e.g., 'client' becomes 'customer' with no explanation). What should happen?

options.text: Nothing; inconsistent terminology never affects clarity
The terminology should be standardized throughout the document for clarity and professionalism, since inconsistent terms can confuse readers
This is a factual error requiring source verification
The document should be rejected entirely and never revised

questions.explanation: Inconsistent terminology is a structural/clarity issue that should simply be standardized during review, not treated as a fatal flaw or a factual error.

questions.stem: Why should a reviewer check whether a document's sections are logically ordered, not just individually well-written?

options.text: Section order never affects how well a document communicates
A logical, well-ordered flow (e.g., background before analysis before recommendation) helps the reader follow and be persuaded by the argument, regardless of individual sentence quality
Order only matters for creative writing
Documents should always be ordered alphabetically by section name

questions.explanation: A logical section order supports the reader's ability to follow and be persuaded by the overall argument.

questions.stem: A document intended to persuade a skeptical audience presents its recommendation first, with supporting evidence buried at the very end. What structural improvement would likely help?

options.text: Reordering to build the case with evidence before the recommendation (or otherwise ensuring the skeptical reader sees the reasoning before being asked to accept the conclusion)
Removing all evidence entirely to shorten the document
No change needed; order never affects persuasiveness
Repeating the recommendation multiple times instead of adding evidence

questions.explanation: For a skeptical audience, evidence-before-conclusion structuring is generally more persuasive than leading with an unsupported claim.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable check for whether a document's claims are appropriately supported?

options.text: Assume all claims are supported if the document is long enough
Verify that each significant claim has either explicit supporting evidence/reasoning in the document or a cited source, rather than being asserted without backing
Claims never need support if they sound reasonable
Only the first claim in a document needs to be checked

questions.explanation: Each significant claim should be traceable to either in-document reasoning/evidence or an external source — unsupported assertions are a structural weakness.

questions.stem: A comparison document rates three vendors, but the written justification section only discusses two of them. What should a careful reviewer flag?

options.text: The document should be discarded and never reused
Nothing; this is a minor and acceptable oversight
The third vendor should be removed from consideration with no further explanation
The missing justification for the third vendor as an incompleteness/consistency gap that should be filled in before the document is used for a decision

questions.explanation: A gap between what's being compared and what's actually justified is a concrete completeness issue that should be caught and fixed.

questions.stem: Why is evaluating structure and logic considered a distinct skill from fact-checking specific claims?

options.text: Fact-checking is a subset of structural evaluation with no separate skill involved
Structure never matters if all facts are correct
A document can be built entirely from accurate individual facts and still have a flawed structure or an unsupported overall conclusion — each requires separate evaluation
They are the same skill and require no distinction

questions.explanation: Accuracy at the fact level doesn't guarantee soundness at the argument/structure level — both need to be checked independently.

questions.stem: A document's introduction promises to cover four topics, but the body only addresses three of them. What is the appropriate fix?

options.text: Either add the missing fourth topic to the body or revise the introduction to accurately reflect what the document actually covers
Add a note apologizing for the omission with no further correction
Delete the introduction entirely
Leave it as-is since three out of four is close enough

questions.explanation: Resolving the mismatch — by completing the content or correcting the promise — restores internal consistency between the introduction and the body.

questions.stem: What does 'SME sign-off' mean in the context of reviewing AI-generated content?

options.text: Formal review and approval by a qualified Subject Matter Expert before high-stakes content (e.g., medical, legal, financial, safety) is finalized or acted upon
Automatic approval granted by the AI system itself
A step that is never necessary regardless of the content's stakes
A generic spell-check performed by any available employee

questions.explanation: SME sign-off is a human, qualified-expert review step specifically reserved for content where errors carry serious consequences.

questions.stem: Claude drafts patient-facing guidance about medication dosages for a healthcare organization. What should happen before this content is distributed?

options.text: SME review is optional and can be skipped to save time
Only a grammar check is needed before distribution
It must be reviewed and formally approved by a qualified medical professional before distribution, given the safety stakes involved
It can be distributed immediately since it reads clearly and confidently

questions.explanation: Medical guidance affecting patient safety requires qualified expert sign-off regardless of how polished or confident the draft reads.

questions.stem: Which category of content is most clearly identified as requiring SME sign-off before use?

options.text: An internal brainstorm list of possible team lunch spots
Medical, legal, financial, or safety-related guidance that could cause real harm if incorrect
A casual internal chat message with no external impact
A first-draft blog post idea with no publication plan

questions.explanation: High-stakes domains where errors cause real harm — medical, legal, financial, safety — are exactly where SME review is expected.

questions.stem: An AI-drafted contract clause will be sent to an external counterparty. What is the appropriate process before sending?

options.text: Have a qualified legal reviewer examine and approve the clause before it is sent externally
Skip legal review since AI-generated text is inherently compliant
Send it directly since it reads as professionally worded
Only check the clause for spelling errors

questions.explanation: External contract language carries legal risk and requires qualified legal review before being sent, regardless of drafting quality.

questions.stem: Why does polished, confident-sounding AI output NOT substitute for SME review in high-stakes domains?

options.text: Polished output is always accurate, so SME review is redundant
Fluency and confidence are stylistic properties that don't guarantee domain-specific correctness or compliance, which only a qualified expert can properly assess
SME review only matters for poorly written content
There is no meaningful difference between polish and correctness

questions.explanation: How something reads has no necessary connection to whether it's actually correct in a specialized, high-stakes domain — that requires genuine expertise to assess.

questions.stem: A financial projection generated with AI assistance will be presented to investors. What is the appropriate sign-off process?

options.text: Present it directly since the calculations appear internally consistent
Have a qualified financial professional review the assumptions, methodology, and figures before the projection is presented externally
Skip review since investors will catch any errors themselves
Only check that the numbers are formatted with correct currency symbols

questions.explanation: Investor-facing financial projections carry real stakes and require qualified financial review of substance, not just formatting.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to decide whether a given piece of AI-assisted content needs SME sign-off?

options.text: SME sign-off is never needed if the content was AI-generated, since AI is assumed reliable
Assess the potential consequences of an error — content where mistakes could cause real financial, legal, medical, or safety harm should get SME review
SME sign-off should be applied uniformly to every single piece of content regardless of stakes
Only content over a certain word count needs SME review

questions.explanation: Risk-based triage — based on the real-world consequences of an error — is the sound way to decide where SME review is warranted.

questions.stem: An internal team uses Claude to draft a low-stakes internal FAQ about office supply ordering. Does this scenario require formal SME sign-off?

options.text: This scenario requires FDA approval
Yes, all AI-generated content requires the same level of formal expert sign-off
No review of any kind is ever appropriate for any AI-generated content
Not necessarily — light-touch internal review may be proportionate, since the consequences of an error here are low compared to medical, legal, financial, or safety content

questions.explanation: Sign-off rigor should scale with actual risk; a low-stakes internal FAQ doesn't carry the same consequences as regulated or safety-critical content.

questions.stem: Who is qualified to provide SME sign-off on a piece of medical guidance content?

options.text: The AI model itself, since it generated the content
Whoever is available fastest, regardless of relevant expertise
Any employee who reads it and feels it sounds correct
A person with genuine, verifiable medical expertise relevant to the specific content being reviewed

questions.explanation: Sign-off requires genuine, relevant expertise — general confidence or availability doesn't substitute for actual qualification.

questions.stem: A legal summary drafted with AI assistance will inform a significant business decision. Who should review it before the decision is finalized?

options.text: No one; the summary can be acted on directly
The original AI system, asked to confirm its own accuracy
A marketing team member with no legal background
A qualified legal professional, to confirm the summary's accuracy and completeness before it informs a significant decision

questions.explanation: A significant decision resting on legal accuracy warrants review by someone with actual legal qualification, not self-review by the AI.

questions.stem: What is the risk of skipping SME sign-off on high-stakes content purely to save time?

options.text: There is no risk; time savings always outweigh review value
Skipping sign-off always improves the content's quality
An undetected error in a high-stakes domain (medical, legal, financial, safety) could cause real harm, liability, or costly consequences that far outweigh the time saved
SME review has no bearing on the actual accuracy of high-stakes content
