questions.explanation: Evaluating actual quality and efficiency outcomes — and adjusting if they fall short — is the practical way to validate an integration decision.

questions.stem: A business process has a legally required review step that cannot be skipped. How should Claude be integrated with respect to this step?

options.text: The legally required step should be removed from the process to simplify integration
Claude should be used to skip or bypass the legally required step entirely
Claude can assist with preparation for that step (e.g., organizing relevant materials), but the legally required review itself must still be performed as mandated
Claude should replace the legally required reviewer entirely

questions.explanation: AI assistance can support preparation for a mandatory step, but cannot substitute for a legally required review itself.

questions.stem: Why might starting with a small, well-defined process step (rather than an entire end-to-end process) be a sound way to begin integrating Claude into business operations?

options.text: Small-scale starts are never useful and should always be skipped
A contained pilot makes it easier to evaluate results, catch issues, and refine the approach before expanding to a larger or more complex scope
Small-scale integration always fails and provides no useful information
Scope size is irrelevant to how successful an integration will be

questions.explanation: A contained, evaluable pilot reduces risk and provides real information to guide a broader rollout.

questions.stem: What is the benefit of designing a multi-step workflow (e.g., research, then draft, then review, then finalize) rather than a single undifferentiated request?

options.text: Multi-step workflows are only relevant to software development
Breaking work into stages always produces a worse final result
Distinct stages create natural checkpoints for review and correction, and each stage can be optimized (and, if needed, reviewed) independently
There is no benefit; a single request is always equally effective for any deliverable

questions.explanation: Clear stages create checkpoints for catching issues early and allow each part of the process to be independently refined.

questions.stem: A team designs a workflow: Claude drafts a report outline, a manager reviews the outline, Claude expands the approved outline into a full draft, then an editor does a final review. What does this design reflect?

options.text: A sound multi-step workflow with review checkpoints placed at key transitions to catch issues before they propagate into larger amounts of work
A poorly designed process with unnecessary steps
A process that should be collapsed into a single step for efficiency
A workflow with no meaningful checkpoints at all

questions.explanation: Checkpoints placed before the outline is expanded, and again before finalization, are well-timed to catch problems before they multiply.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to place a review checkpoint BEFORE a large amount of downstream work depends on an earlier stage's output?

options.text: Placing checkpoints earlier always slows down the overall process with no benefit
Checkpoint placement never matters; timing has no effect on efficiency
Checkpoints are only useful at the very end of a workflow, never earlier
Catching an error at an early, foundational stage prevents wasted effort building additional work on top of a flawed foundation

questions.explanation: Catching foundational errors early avoids the wasted effort of building substantial additional work on top of a flawed base.

questions.stem: A workflow chains together: data extraction, then analysis, then recommendation drafting. If the extraction step contains an error, what happens without a checkpoint after that stage?

options.text: This scenario is not actually possible in a multi-step workflow
Later stages automatically detect and fix any earlier errors with no design needed
The error is likely to propagate into the analysis and recommendation stages, potentially undermining the entire final output
The error has no effect on later stages

questions.explanation: In a chained workflow, an uncaught early-stage error tends to propagate forward, corrupting everything built on top of it.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable principle for deciding how many distinct stages a multi-step workflow should have?

options.text: Always use exactly one single stage regardless of complexity
The number of stages should be chosen at random
Enough stages to create meaningful checkpoints at genuinely important transitions, without adding so many trivial stages that the process becomes needlessly slow
Always maximize the number of stages regardless of the task's actual complexity

questions.explanation: The right number of stages balances catching real risks at meaningful transitions against unnecessary process overhead.

questions.stem: A workflow for producing a client deliverable includes a stage where a draft is checked against the original requirements before final formatting. What purpose does this stage serve?

options.text: It exists only to slow down the process with no other function
No real purpose; it can be removed without any effect
It replaces the need for any other review in the workflow
It verifies the draft actually satisfies what was originally requested before time is spent on final polish, catching misalignment early

questions.explanation: Verifying alignment with original requirements before investing in final formatting avoids polishing a draft that doesn't actually meet the need.

questions.stem: Why might a workflow separate 'drafting' and 'fact-checking' into two distinct stages rather than combining them into one step?

options.text: There is no reason to separate these two activities
Separating them allows focused attention on each distinct type of work — generating content versus verifying it — rather than trying to do both simultaneously
Fact-checking is never necessary in a well-designed workflow
Drafting and fact-checking are identical activities requiring no distinction

questions.explanation: Distinct stages let each type of work get focused attention, rather than blending generation and verification in a way that can shortchange both.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of setting custom instructions at the Project level?

options.text: To establish standing guidance (tone, format, constraints, conventions) that automatically applies to every conversation within that Project
To disable all conversations within the Project
To restrict the Project to a single user forever
To permanently delete the project

questions.explanation: Project-level custom instructions provide standing, automatically-applied guidance so it doesn't need to be repeated in every conversation.

questions.stem: A team wants every conversation in a specific Project to consistently follow their brand voice guidelines. What is the most efficient way to achieve this?

options.text: Manually re-explain the brand voice guidelines in every single new conversation
Set the brand voice guidelines as a custom instruction at the Project level, so they apply automatically across all conversations in that Project
Avoid using Projects and hope for consistency by chance
Set the guidelines as a one-time instruction that only applies to the very first conversation

questions.explanation: Project-level custom instructions apply automatically and consistently across every conversation in that Project, removing the need for manual repetition.

questions.stem: What happens to custom instructions set at the Project level when a new conversation is started within that Project?

options.text: They must be manually re-entered for the new conversation
They automatically apply to the new conversation without needing to be re-entered
They are permanently deleted
They only apply to conversations started on the same calendar day

questions.explanation: Project-level instructions persist and automatically apply to new conversations created within that Project.

questions.stem: A user sets up a Project for a specific client account, including relevant background and preferences as custom instructions. What is the main benefit for future work on that account?

options.text: No benefit; instructions must still be repeated in every conversation regardless
This setup only works for a single conversation and then must be redone
Future conversations about that client can start with the relevant context already in place, avoiding repetitive re-explanation
This setup actively prevents any future conversations about the client

questions.explanation: Persisted client-specific context in a Project saves the repetitive re-explanation that separate, unconfigured conversations would require.

questions.stem: Why might an organization want multiple separate Projects rather than one single Project for everything?

options.text: There is no meaningful difference between using one Project or many
Multiple Projects are never useful; one Project should always be used for everything
Projects are limited to exactly one conversation each, making multiple Projects mandatory
Separate Projects let different bodies of work have their own tailored context, instructions, and knowledge sources without one project's settings interfering with another's

questions.explanation: Distinct Projects keep unrelated bodies of work cleanly separated, each with its own appropriate context and instructions.

questions.stem: A user wants a Project's custom instructions to specify a particular output format for all reports generated within it. What is the appropriate approach?

options.text: Manually specify the format in every single individual conversation, ignoring the Project-level option
This kind of standing preference cannot be configured at the Project level
Assume format will be consistent automatically with no configuration
Include the desired format specification as part of the Project's custom instructions

questions.explanation: Standing format preferences for all work within a Project are exactly what Project-level custom instructions are designed to capture.

questions.stem: What is a good practice when writing custom instructions for a Project?

options.text: Make them as vague as possible to maximize flexibility
Make them clear and specific about the standing context, tone, format, or constraints that should apply, similar to good prompt-writing principles
Custom instructions should never mention format or tone
Custom instructions should be written in a language different from the conversations that will use them

questions.explanation: The same clarity and specificity principles that make individual prompts effective also make Project-level instructions effective.

questions.stem: A Project's custom instructions become outdated after a company rebrand. What should happen?

options.text: Update the Project's custom instructions to reflect the new branding, so future conversations in that Project stay consistent with current guidelines
Delete the entire Project and never use Projects again
Ignore the mismatch since it won't affect anything
Leave the outdated instructions in place indefinitely

questions.explanation: Custom instructions should be kept current — updating them after a meaningful change like a rebrand keeps future outputs aligned with reality.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of adding knowledge sources (reference documents/files) to a Claude Project?

options.text: To give conversations within that Project direct access to specific reference material, so responses can be grounded in that material rather than general knowledge alone
To prevent the Project from being used for any future conversations
To permanently increase the cost of every conversation with no benefit
To automatically publish the documents publicly

questions.explanation: Knowledge sources ground a Project's conversations in specific, relevant reference material rather than relying solely on general background knowledge.

questions.stem: A team wants every conversation in a Project to be able to reference their internal policy handbook without re-uploading it each time. What is the appropriate configuration?

options.text: Upload the handbook as a knowledge source within the Project, so it's available across all conversations in that Project
Re-upload the handbook manually in every new conversation
Avoid using the handbook at all going forward
Print the handbook and read it aloud during each conversation

questions.explanation: Adding a knowledge source at the Project level makes it persistently available without repeated manual uploading.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep knowledge sources within a Project up to date?

options.text: Knowledge sources never need updating once added
Outdated knowledge sources can lead to responses grounded in stale or incorrect information, undermining the accuracy benefit of configuring them in the first place
Knowledge sources automatically update themselves with no user action
Updating knowledge sources always reduces response quality

questions.explanation: The value of grounding responses in reference material depends on that material being accurate and current — stale sources undermine that benefit.

questions.stem: A Project's knowledge sources include an old version of a pricing sheet that has since changed. What risk does this create?

options.text: No risk; Claude will automatically know the pricing has changed
Responses grounded in the outdated pricing sheet could confidently present incorrect, outdated prices as if they were current
This risk only applies to legal documents, never pricing
The outdated document will be automatically ignored

questions.explanation: An outdated knowledge source can be used to generate confidently-stated but incorrect current information, exactly the kind of risk configuration upkeep is meant to prevent.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable practice for organizing knowledge sources across multiple Projects?

options.text: Add only the documents genuinely relevant to that Project's specific purpose, keeping each Project's knowledge base focused and relevant
Randomly assign documents to Projects with no consideration of relevance
Never add any knowledge sources to any Project
Add every document from the entire organization to every single Project regardless of relevance

questions.explanation: Focused, relevant knowledge sources per Project keep responses grounded in what's actually pertinent, rather than diluted by irrelevant material.

questions.stem: A user notices Claude's responses within a Project seem to be missing key information that should be available. What is a reasonable first check?

options.text: Assume Claude is malfunctioning with no further investigation
Assume the missing information can never be added
Delete the entire Project immediately
Verify that the relevant document has actually been added as a knowledge source to that Project and is current

questions.explanation: Checking whether the relevant material is actually configured as a knowledge source is the direct, practical first troubleshooting step.

questions.stem: Why might sensitive or confidential documents require extra consideration before being added as knowledge sources?

options.text: Sensitive documents should always be added with no additional consideration
Knowledge sources can never contain any sensitive information under any circumstances
Sensitivity is irrelevant to knowledge source configuration decisions
Adding sensitive material makes it accessible within that Project's conversations, so appropriate access controls and organizational policy should be considered before doing so

questions.explanation: Because knowledge sources become accessible within a Project's conversations, sensitivity and access-control considerations should inform the decision to add them.

questions.stem: A Project needs to reference both a large reference manual and a short internal glossary. What is a reasonable configuration approach?

options.text: Avoid adding any knowledge sources since more than one document is involved
Add only one of the two documents, arbitrarily discarding the other
Add both relevant documents as knowledge sources, since both provide genuinely useful reference material for the Project's purpose
Combine both documents into a single unreadable file before adding either

questions.explanation: Multiple genuinely relevant reference documents can all be added as knowledge sources to support the Project's actual needs.

questions.stem: When a conversation-level instruction conflicts with a Project-level custom instruction, what is a reasonable general expectation?

options.text: Conflicts of this kind can never occur
More specific, conversation-level instructions generally take precedence for that specific conversation, while the Project-level instruction continues to apply as the default elsewhere
Project-level instructions always completely override anything said in an individual conversation with no exception
Whichever instruction was typed in a larger font automatically wins

questions.explanation: More specific, immediate instructions for a given conversation generally take precedence over standing defaults, without erasing those defaults for other conversations.

questions.stem: A Project's custom instructions specify a formal tone by default, but a user asks for a specific response in a more casual tone for one particular request. What should happen?

options.text: The Project's default instructions should be permanently deleted because of this one request
The formal default should be rigidly enforced with no exception ever possible
The specific, explicit request for a casual tone in that conversation should generally be honored for that request, without needing to change the Project's overall default
The request should be entirely ignored since it conflicts with the Project default

questions.explanation: An explicit, specific instruction for a given conversation can reasonably override a standing default for that instance, without requiring a permanent change.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to understand which level (Project vs. individual conversation) an instruction is set at?

options.text: Understanding scope helps predict which conversations an instruction will affect, and helps troubleshoot unexpected behavior if instructions from different levels appear to conflict
It's never useful; all instructions behave identically regardless of level
Instructions set at any level always apply to every Project simultaneously
Scope only matters for developers, never for business users

questions.explanation: Understanding scope is what allows a user to predict behavior and troubleshoot conflicts between standing defaults and specific requests.

questions.stem: A user is confused why a particular conversation isn't following a formatting rule they thought was standard. What is a reasonable diagnostic step?

options.text: Delete the conversation immediately with no diagnosis
Assume the system is broken with no further investigation
Check whether that formatting rule was actually set as a Project-level custom instruction (versus just assumed or mentioned once in an unrelated past conversation)
Assume formatting rules can never be configured at all

questions.explanation: Confirming whether the expected rule was actually persisted at the Project level (versus a one-off past mention) is the direct way to diagnose this kind of confusion.

questions.stem: What is a practical benefit of explicitly documenting what's configured at the Project level (instructions, knowledge sources) for a team?

options.text: No benefit; team members should just guess at what's configured
It helps team members understand what context and rules are already in place, avoiding both unnecessary repetition and confusion about unexpected behavior
Documentation is only useful for very large organizations
This kind of documentation actively causes more confusion

questions.explanation: Clear documentation of Project-level configuration helps a team use it consistently and troubleshoot effectively.

questions.stem: Two different Projects have conflicting custom instructions about formatting. What is the expected behavior?

options.text: Each Project's instructions apply independently within that specific Project, with no interference between the two separate Projects
Whichever Project was created first overrides the other permanently
The instructions merge into a single, contradictory rule applied everywhere
The conflicting instructions will cause both Projects to stop working entirely

questions.explanation: Projects operate independently — each one's configuration applies within its own scope without cross-contaminating another Project.

questions.stem: Why might a team benefit from a shared Project rather than each member maintaining separate, disconnected configurations for the same body of work?

options.text: A shared Project ensures everyone works from the same context, instructions, and knowledge sources, improving consistency across the team's output
Shared Projects prevent any team member from using Claude at all
Individual, disconnected setups always guarantee better consistency than a shared Project
There is no benefit; shared Projects always perform worse than individual setups

questions.explanation: Shared configuration is what actually produces consistent output and shared context across a team working on the same body of work.

questions.stem: A marketing team wants everyone drafting client-facing content to follow the same brand guidelines and reference the same approved messaging documents. What is a sound way to organize this?

options.text: Avoid any shared configuration and rely on memory alone
Have each team member independently maintain their own separate, unsynced version of the guidelines
Prohibit the marketing team from using Claude at all
Set up a shared Project with the brand guidelines as a custom instruction and the messaging documents as shared knowledge sources

questions.explanation: A shared Project with consistent instructions and knowledge sources is the direct way to keep an entire team aligned on guidelines and messaging.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to decide whether a new body of work should get its own dedicated Project versus being added to an existing one?

options.text: Always create a new Project for absolutely everything, regardless of overlap with existing work
Consider whether the new work shares meaningful context/instructions/knowledge sources with an existing Project, or represents a genuinely distinct body of work warranting its own setup
Never create more than one Project total for an entire organization
The decision should be made randomly with no consideration of context overlap

questions.explanation: Assessing genuine overlap in context and purpose is the practical basis for deciding whether to reuse or create a new Project.

questions.stem: A large organization has many small teams, each working on distinct clients with different requirements. What is a reasonable Project structure?

options.text: No Projects at all; every conversation should be unconfigured
One single Project shared across the entire organization regardless of client differences
A new Project created for every single individual conversation regardless of overlap
Separate Projects per client/team, each configured with the context, instructions, and knowledge sources relevant to that specific body of work

questions.explanation: Distinct clients with different requirements are well-served by separate, appropriately-scoped Projects rather than one undifferentiated shared setup or excessive fragmentation.

questions.stem: Why is periodic review of a team's Project configuration (instructions and knowledge sources) a good practice?

options.text: Review is never necessary once a Project is initially set up
Team needs, branding, policies, and reference materials change over time, so periodic review helps ensure the configuration stays accurate and useful
Reviewing Project configuration always makes things worse
Only brand-new Projects ever need any kind of review

questions.explanation: Business context evolves, so periodic review keeps a Project's standing configuration aligned with current reality rather than growing stale.

questions.stem: Before pasting a customer's full credit card number into a chat with Claude, what should a responsible business user consider?

options.text: Nothing; a customer's full credit card number can always be shared freely with no consideration
Whether sharing it will make the response longer
Whether the information is interesting enough to share
Whether the organization's data-handling policy and any applicable privacy/legal obligations permit sharing this category of sensitive information in this context

questions.explanation: Sensitive personal, financial, health, or confidential information should be evaluated against organizational policy and applicable legal obligations before being shared in any AI tool.

questions.stem: Why should users generally be cautious about inputting sensitive personal or confidential business data into any AI chat tool?

options.text: There is never any reason for caution regardless of data sensitivity
Data handling, retention, and privacy implications vary by product/settings, and sensitive data deserves deliberate consideration of applicable policies before being shared
Caution is only relevant for government employees
AI tools are legally prohibited from processing any text input whatsoever

questions.explanation: Responsible handling of sensitive data starts with deliberately considering applicable privacy/policy implications rather than sharing by default.

questions.stem: An employee wants to know how their organization's model-improvement or data-retention settings affect information shared in chats. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Guess based on personal assumption with no verification
Review the organization's specific privacy/data-handling settings and policy documentation, or ask an administrator, rather than assuming
Assume all organizations have identical settings with no variation
Avoid ever asking about this topic

questions.explanation: Data handling and retention settings can vary, so checking actual policy/settings (or asking an administrator) is the responsible approach rather than assuming.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable default approach when uncertain whether a specific piece of information is too sensitive to share in a chat?

options.text: Share as much sensitive information as possible to be thorough
Uncertainty is never a reason to pause before sharing information
Err on the side of caution — omit or anonymize the sensitive detail, or check with a relevant policy/administrator before sharing
Share it anyway since uncertainty means it's probably fine

questions.explanation: When genuinely uncertain, erring toward caution (omitting, anonymizing, or checking first) is the safer default than sharing and hoping it's fine.

questions.stem: A user needs Claude's help with a task involving customer data but doesn't need every individual field to complete it. What is a privacy-conscious approach?

options.text: Share the entire customer database unnecessarily, including irrelevant sensitive fields
Share only the specific fields actually necessary for the task, omitting or anonymizing unrelated sensitive details
Privacy considerations are irrelevant as long as the task gets done
Always share the maximum possible amount of data regardless of necessity

questions.explanation: Sharing only what's necessary for the task (data minimization) is a core responsible-use practice for handling sensitive information.

questions.stem: Why might different organizations have different policies about what data can be shared with Claude?

options.text: Policy differences are always arbitrary and never based on real considerations
All organizations are legally required to have identical policies
Data-handling policy never actually varies between organizations
Organizations operate under different regulatory obligations, risk tolerances, and industries, leading to legitimately different data-handling policies

questions.explanation: Different regulatory contexts, industries, and risk profiles legitimately lead to different organizational policies on data sharing.

questions.stem: A user is drafting a document that references a real client by name along with sensitive deal details. What is a privacy-conscious practice before sharing this in a chat?

options.text: Include all real names and sensitive details with no consideration
Consider whether the task actually requires the real client name and full sensitive details, or whether a placeholder/anonymized version would suffice
Always use real, unredacted details regardless of necessity
Refuse to work on any document involving client information under any circumstances

questions.explanation: Considering whether real identifying/sensitive details are actually necessary — versus a placeholder — is a practical way to reduce unnecessary exposure.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable question to ask before sharing any sensitive data with an AI tool as part of a work task?

options.text: Will sharing this data make the response arrive faster?
Will this make my message longer?
Is this data interesting?
Does this violate my organization's data-handling policy or applicable regulations?

questions.explanation: Policy and regulatory compliance is the directly relevant question — message length, interest level, and response speed are irrelevant to the privacy consideration.

questions.stem: A regulated industry (e.g., healthcare or finance) employee is considering using Claude for a task involving regulated client data. What should inform their decision?

options.text: Personal preference alone, with no regard for industry-specific regulations
The specific regulatory requirements applicable to their industry and organization, in addition to general good data-handling practice
Regulations never apply to AI tool usage in any industry
The decision should be made with no reference to any regulatory considerations

questions.explanation: Regulated industries carry specific compliance obligations that must inform decisions about what data can appropriately be used with any tool, including AI.

questions.stem: What does 'responsible AI use' generally mean in a business context?

options.text: Always fully automating every decision with AI regardless of stakes
Refusing to use AI tools under any circumstances
Using AI tools without any consideration of accuracy, fairness, or appropriate application
Using AI thoughtfully — verifying outputs, respecting privacy, avoiding inappropriate reliance on AI for decisions beyond its appropriate scope, and being transparent about AI's role where relevant

questions.explanation: Responsible use is a set of practical habits — verification, privacy awareness, appropriate scoping, and transparency — not blanket avoidance or blanket automation.

questions.stem: A team is using Claude to help screen job candidates. What responsible-use consideration is most important here?

options.text: None; hiring decisions can be fully automated with no oversight
AI-assisted screening requires no verification of any kind
Speed is the only consideration that matters in hiring
Being aware of potential bias in AI-assisted screening, keeping meaningful human judgment in the final decision, and ensuring the process is fair and compliant with applicable employment laws

questions.explanation: Hiring carries fairness, legal, and bias considerations that require human oversight and awareness, not full unsupervised automation.

questions.stem: Why is it important to be aware that AI-generated content can reflect biases present in its training data or patterns?

options.text: AI is always perfectly neutral and unbiased in every context
Being aware of potential bias helps users critically evaluate outputs (e.g., in hiring, evaluations, or recommendations) rather than assuming automatic neutrality
Bias awareness is irrelevant to responsible business use
This concern only applies to image-generating AI tools

questions.explanation: Awareness of potential bias supports critical evaluation of AI outputs in sensitive contexts, rather than assuming outputs are automatically neutral.

questions.stem: A manager plans to use an AI-generated performance summary as the sole basis for a promotion decision with no additional human judgment. What is the concern?

options.text: Consequential personnel decisions warrant meaningful human judgment and context beyond a single AI-generated summary, given the stakes and potential for bias or error
This concern is irrelevant to responsible AI use
AI-generated summaries are always more objective than human judgment and should always be the sole basis for such decisions
There is no concern; this is a fully appropriate use of AI

questions.explanation: High-stakes personnel decisions deserve human judgment informed by broader context, not sole reliance on a single AI-generated artifact.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable principle regarding transparency about AI's role in business communications or decisions?

options.text: Being appropriately transparent about where and how AI assistance was used supports trust and accountability, particularly for decisions that affect other people
Transparency requirements are identical in every possible situation with no variation
AI's role should always be actively concealed from anyone affected by a decision
Transparency about AI use is never relevant in any business context

questions.explanation: Appropriate transparency about AI's role supports trust and accountability, especially where a decision meaningfully affects someone else.

questions.stem: A company uses Claude to draft responses to sensitive customer complaints. What responsible-use practice is most relevant here?

options.text: Having a human review and personalize sensitive responses before sending, given the potential impact on the customer relationship
Sending AI-drafted responses directly with no human review, regardless of complaint sensitivity
Refusing to use AI assistance for any customer-facing task
Responsible use principles don't apply to customer service contexts

questions.explanation: Human review before sending sensitive, relationship-affecting communications is a proportionate responsible-use practice, distinct from either full automation or blanket avoidance.

questions.stem: Why does responsible AI use generally call for scaling the level of scrutiny to the stakes of the task?

options.text: Higher-stakes tasks (affecting people's finances, rights, health, or safety) carry more potential for harm if something goes wrong, warranting proportionally more careful use and review
All tasks warrant identical scrutiny regardless of their consequences
Stakes have no bearing on how AI-assisted work should be reviewed
Scrutiny should be inversely related to stakes, with low-stakes tasks requiring the most review

questions.explanation: Proportional scrutiny — more care for higher-consequence tasks — is a practical, efficient application of responsible-use principles.

questions.stem: An organization wants to establish internal guidelines for responsible AI use. Which topic should such guidelines reasonably address?

options.text: Only the cost of the AI subscription plan
Guidelines should avoid mentioning data handling or review requirements entirely
Appropriate data handling, required human review for high-stakes outputs, and expectations around verifying AI-generated content before relying on it
Only the visual theme of the AI chat interface

questions.explanation: Substantive responsible-use guidelines address data handling, review requirements, and verification expectations — not just cosmetic or purely financial details.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable general signal that a task should be escalated to a human expert rather than handled solely with AI assistance?

options.text: The task involves specialized expertise, significant consequences if wrong, or a domain (medical, legal, financial, safety) where qualified judgment is required
The task involves any text at all
The task took more than five minutes
The task involves more than one paragraph of text

questions.explanation: Specialized expertise requirements and significant consequence potential are the meaningful signals for escalation, not task length or time spent.

questions.stem: While using Claude to draft a response to a customer, a user encounters a legal threat embedded in the customer's message. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Ignore the legal threat entirely and proceed as if it wasn't mentioned
Have Claude draft a response and send it immediately with no further involvement
Escalate the situation to a qualified person (e.g., legal or a manager) rather than resolving it solely through an AI-drafted customer response
Ask Claude to handle the entire matter with no human involvement at all

questions.explanation: A legal threat is exactly the kind of situation that calls for escalation to a qualified human rather than being resolved solely via an AI-assisted response.

questions.stem: Why is recognizing the limits of AI assistance an important responsible-use skill?

options.text: Recognizing limits is unnecessary since AI always knows when to escalate on its own
This skill is only relevant to technical AI developers, not everyday business users
Some situations require human expertise, authority, or judgment that AI assistance cannot appropriately substitute for, and recognizing these cases prevents inappropriate over-reliance
AI has no limits and can appropriately handle every possible situation independently

questions.explanation: Understanding where AI assistance stops being appropriate — and human expertise/authority is required — is central to using AI responsibly rather than over-relying on it.

questions.stem: A user asks Claude for guidance on a situation that appears to involve a serious safety hazard at their workplace. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Rely solely on Claude's general guidance with no further action
Treat this as a signal to escalate to the appropriate workplace safety personnel or authority, using any AI-provided general guidance as a supplement, not a replacement, for proper escalation
Ignore the situation since it was only mentioned in an AI chat
Assume no further action is needed once general guidance has been given

questions.explanation: Serious safety hazards call for real escalation to qualified safety personnel — AI guidance can supplement but not substitute for that.

questions.stem: Which of these scenarios most clearly calls for human escalation rather than continued AI-only assistance?

options.text: Formatting a routine internal memo
Drafting a routine meeting agenda
A situation involving a potential regulatory violation with significant legal exposure for the organization
Brainstorming names for an internal project

questions.explanation: Significant legal/regulatory exposure is a clear, high-stakes signal for escalation to qualified human expertise.

questions.stem: An employee is using Claude to draft an internal message but the underlying situation involves a potential conflict of interest they're unsure how to handle. What is the appropriate step?

options.text: Have Claude resolve the conflict of interest question directly with no further human involvement
Ignore the conflict of interest since it wasn't the original request
Assume AI assistance eliminates the need for any organizational escalation process

Escalate the underlying conflict-of-interest question to the appropriate internal function (e.g., compliance, HR, or a manager) rather than treating an AI-drafted message as a substitute for that judgment call

questions.explanation: A substantive conflict-of-interest question is an organizational judgment call requiring the appropriate human function, not something to be resolved via AI-drafted text alone.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable relationship between an organization's escalation policies and its use of AI tools?

options.text: AI tool adoption eliminates the need for any existing escalation policies
There is no meaningful relationship between the two
Existing escalation policies (for legal, safety, compliance, etc. issues) should continue to apply regardless of whether AI assistance was used in drafting related content
Escalation policies only apply to fully manual work, never AI-assisted work

questions.explanation: The presence of AI assistance in drafting doesn't change whether an underlying situation requires the organization's normal escalation process.

questions.stem: A user is unsure whether a situation is serious enough to warrant escalation. What is a reasonable default approach?

options.text: Flip a coin to decide
Assume it's never serious enough and proceed without escalation
When genuinely uncertain about a potentially significant issue (legal, safety, compliance), err toward raising it with the appropriate person rather than assuming it's fine
Escalate literally everything regardless of any judgment about severity

questions.explanation: Given the asymmetric cost of missing a genuinely serious issue, erring toward raising uncertain cases is the safer default.

questions.stem: How should a routine internal meeting agenda generally be categorized in terms of risk level for AI-assisted content?

options.text: Low risk
Risk level cannot be assessed for any type of content
All content should always be treated as the same risk level regardless of context
Risk level is determined solely by the length of the content

questions.explanation: This type of content is generally considered low risk based on its potential consequences if something in it is wrong, which should inform how much review it receives.

questions.stem: How should a public regulatory filing generally be categorized in terms of risk level for AI-assisted content?

options.text: Risk level cannot be assessed for any type of content
All content should always be treated as the same risk level regardless of context
High risk
Risk level is determined solely by the length of the content

questions.explanation: This type of content is generally considered high risk based on its potential consequences if something in it is wrong, which should inform how much review it receives.

questions.stem: What is the practical purpose of categorizing content by risk level (e.g., low, medium, high stakes)?

options.text: It helps determine an appropriate, proportional level of review, verification, and escalation for each specific piece of content, rather than treating everything identically
Risk categorization is only relevant for very large enterprises
All content should receive the maximum possible level of scrutiny regardless of category
Risk categorization serves no practical purpose in a business workflow

questions.explanation: Risk categorization enables proportional review — the practical goal of distinguishing risk levels in the first place.

questions.stem: Which factor should most influence whether content is categorized as high-stakes?

options.text: The potential real-world consequences (financial, legal, medical, safety, reputational) if the content turns out to be wrong or inappropriate
The specific time of day the content was created
How long the content took to generate
Whether the content includes any bullet points

questions.explanation: Potential real-world consequences of an error are the substantive basis for risk categorization, not superficial factors like length, formatting, or timing.

questions.stem: Why might the same type of content (e.g., a written explanation) fall into different risk categories depending on context?

options.text: Risk category is entirely random and unrelated to context
Content type alone always determines risk category regardless of context
The actual consequences of an error depend heavily on context — the same kind of written explanation could be low-stakes internally but high-stakes if sent externally to regulators or customers
Written explanations are always categorized as high-stakes regardless of audience

questions.explanation: Audience and consequence context — not just content type — determine actual risk level, so the same content type can fall into different categories.

questions.stem: A team is deciding how much review a piece of content needs. Which approach reflects sound risk categorization practice?

options.text: Assess the content's actual potential consequences and apply a proportionally appropriate level of review — lighter for low-stakes content, more rigorous for high-stakes content
Apply the exact same fixed review process to every piece of content regardless of its actual stakes
Skip review entirely for all content regardless of stakes
Apply maximum review effort to literally everything, including trivial content

questions.explanation: Proportional review based on genuine assessed risk is more sound and efficient than either uniform minimal review or uniform maximal review.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to build a consistent risk-categorization habit across a team or organization?

options.text: Leave risk categorization entirely to individual, unguided judgment with no shared framework
Avoid any form of categorization since it's inherently subjective
Categorize risk based solely on which department created the content
Establish clear, shared criteria for what counts as low/medium/high risk content, so categorization is applied consistently rather than varying arbitrarily by individual

questions.explanation: Shared, explicit criteria support consistent categorization across a team, rather than leaving it to unguided individual judgment.

questions.stem: Why should an employee check their organization's specific AI usage policy rather than relying solely on general best practices?

options.text: Organizational policies are always identical to whatever an individual employee personally prefers
Checking organizational policy is never necessary if the employee feels confident
Organizational policies never differ from general best practices
Organizations may have specific rules (e.g., approved use cases, data restrictions, required disclosures) that go beyond or differ from general guidance, based on their industry and risk profile

questions.explanation: Specific organizational rules can add requirements or restrictions beyond generic best practice, based on that organization's particular context.

questions.stem: An employee wants to use Claude for a new type of task not explicitly addressed in their organization's existing AI policy. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Proceed without any further consideration since the policy doesn't explicitly forbid it
Check with the appropriate internal contact (e.g., a manager or compliance function) about whether this use case is appropriate, given it isn't explicitly covered
Assume all uses are automatically approved unless explicitly and individually forbidden
Avoid ever using Claude again due to the ambiguity

questions.explanation: When a policy doesn't clearly address a specific use case, checking with the appropriate internal contact is more responsible than assuming automatic approval.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable purpose of an organization's AI usage policy?

options.text: To establish clear, consistent expectations for appropriate use, data handling, and review requirements across the organization
To ensure every employee uses AI in an identical, undifferentiated way regardless of role
To prevent any use of AI tools under any circumstances
AI usage policies serve no meaningful purpose and can be safely ignored

questions.explanation: A well-designed policy establishes consistent, clear expectations tailored to the organization's actual risk profile and needs — not blanket prohibition or undifferentiated uniformity.

questions.stem: An employee is aware of a colleague using Claude in a way that appears to violate the organization's data-handling policy. What is a reasonable action?

options.text: Ignore the situation entirely with no action taken
Raise the concern through the appropriate internal channel (e.g., a manager or compliance contact), consistent with how other policy concerns would normally be handled
Publicly confront the colleague in a way unrelated to normal organizational processes
Assume policy violations involving AI tools are never worth reporting

questions.explanation: A policy concern involving AI use should be handled the same way other policy concerns are — through appropriate internal channels, not ignored or handled outside normal process.

questions.stem: Why might an organization's AI policy specify approved use cases rather than leaving all usage entirely open-ended?

options.text: Specifying approved use cases is always unnecessary and overly restrictive with no benefit
Clearly scoping appropriate use cases helps manage risk (data exposure, compliance, quality) while still enabling productive use within those boundaries
Approved use cases are only relevant for the technology department
Open-ended usage always poses zero risk to an organization

questions.explanation: Defining approved use cases is a practical risk-management tool that still allows productive use within clear, sensible boundaries.

questions.stem: A new employee is unsure what their organization's policy says about using Claude for client-facing work. What is the appropriate first step?

options.text: Assume no policy exists simply because they haven't seen it yet
Guess based on what other companies might do
Avoid using Claude for any work indefinitely
Locate and review the organization's actual AI usage policy, or ask a manager/compliance contact directly, rather than assuming

questions.explanation: Directly locating the actual policy or asking the right internal contact is more reliable than guessing or assuming.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable relationship between industry-specific regulation and an organization's internal AI policy?

options.text: An organization's internal AI policy often needs to reflect and help ensure compliance with applicable industry-specific regulations
Industry regulation only applies to non-AI tools
Internal policy is always completely unrelated to industry regulation
Internal policy always supersedes and overrides industry regulation

questions.explanation: Internal policy in regulated industries typically needs to operationalize compliance with the relevant external regulatory requirements.

questions.stem: An organization updates its AI usage policy to add new data-handling restrictions. What should employees do?

options.text: Only follow the updated policy if it happens to be more convenient than the old one
Continue following the old policy indefinitely since it's more familiar
Ignore policy updates entirely
Review and adhere to the updated policy, since it reflects the organization's current expectations and compliance requirements

questions.explanation: Following the current, updated policy — not the outdated version — is the expected standard once a policy has been revised.

questions.stem: A response stops abruptly mid-sentence with no natural conclusion. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Claude has permanently stopped functioning
The response likely hit a maximum output length limit before finishing
The user's internet connection caused the sentence to disappear
This behavior is intentional and cannot be addressed

questions.explanation: Abrupt mid-sentence cutoffs are the classic symptom of hitting an output length limit, not a malfunction.

questions.stem: A response is cut off before completing a long list. What is the most direct way to get the rest of the content?

options.text: Rewrite the entire request in a different language
Start an entirely new, unrelated conversation
Ask Claude to 'continue' or pick up where it left off, so the remaining content can be generated
Assume the remaining content is permanently lost with no way to retrieve it

questions.explanation: Simply asking Claude to continue from where it stopped is the direct, practical fix for a length-limited cutoff.

questions.stem: Why might breaking a very large requested output into smaller, sequential requests help avoid truncation issues?

options.text: Breaking requests into smaller pieces has no effect on truncation
Smaller requests always take longer to complete with no other benefit
Truncation only ever happens with short requests, never long ones
Each smaller piece is less likely to hit the length limit on its own, since the total amount of content per individual response is reduced

questions.explanation: Reducing the amount of content requested per individual response reduces the chance any single response hits the length ceiling.

questions.stem: A user needs an extremely long, detailed document generated in full. What is a practical strategy to avoid repeated truncation?

options.text: Request the entire document in one massive prompt and hope it completes without being cut off
Break the document into logical sections and request them one at a time, assembling the final result from the completed parts
Give up on generating long documents entirely
Request the document be written in a smaller font to reduce its length

questions.explanation: Sectioning a very large document into manageable pieces is a practical, effective way to avoid repeated truncation on any single response.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable sign that a task might be too large for a single response and should be broken up preemptively?

options.text: The task requires an extremely long, detailed piece of content (e.g., a lengthy multi-section report) that historically tends to run into length limits
Only tasks involving numbers ever hit length limits
The task is a simple one-sentence question
Task size is never a meaningful signal for anything

questions.explanation: Recognizing that a very large deliverable is likely to approach output limits allows for proactive chunking rather than reactive fixes after truncation occurs.

questions.stem: After a truncated response is continued and completed, what should a careful user do before using the combined content?

options.text: Assume the two parts combine perfectly with no need to check
Review the transition point between the original and continued content to confirm it flows correctly and nothing was duplicated or lost
Discard the continued portion entirely
Ignore the transition point since it never causes issues

questions.explanation: Checking the seam between the original and continued portions is a quick, worthwhile step to catch any duplication or gap introduced by the continuation.

questions.stem: Why might a very large input document need to be broken into smaller chunks before being processed?

options.text: Document size never affects how it can be processed
Chunking is only relevant for image files, never text documents
Extremely large documents may exceed practical context limits, making it necessary to process them in smaller, manageable sections
All documents, regardless of size, are processed identically with no limits

questions.explanation: Very large documents can exceed practical context limits, making chunking into smaller sections a necessary workaround.

questions.stem: A user needs Claude to analyze an extremely long document that exceeds what can be processed at once. What is a practical approach?

options.text: Split the document into logical, meaningful sections and analyze each in turn, then synthesize the section-level results into an overall conclusion
Assume Claude will automatically handle documents of unlimited size with no adjustment
Give up on analyzing the document at all
Delete most of the document randomly until it fits, regardless of what's removed

questions.explanation: Splitting by logical sections and synthesizing afterward is a sound way to handle documents that exceed single-pass processing limits.

questions.stem: What is an important consideration when deciding where to split a large document into chunks?

options.text: Documents should always be split into exactly two equal halves regardless of content
Splitting should always occur in the middle of sentences for consistency
Splitting at logical boundaries (e.g., sections, chapters) rather than arbitrary midpoints helps preserve coherent meaning within each chunk
Splitting location is irrelevant; any split point works equally well

questions.explanation: Splitting at logical boundaries preserves the coherence of each chunk, making analysis more reliable than arbitrary or mid-sentence splits.

questions.stem: After analyzing a large document in several chunks, what is an important final step?

options.text: Discard all but the first chunk's analysis
Assume the chunks never need to be combined for any purpose
Treat each chunk's analysis as entirely separate with no need to reconcile them
Synthesize the individual chunk analyses into a coherent overall summary or conclusion, checking for consistency across chunks

questions.explanation: A final synthesis step ties the individual chunk-level analyses back together into one coherent overall result.

questions.stem: Why might important context be lost if a document is chunked without any overlap or connecting summary between chunks?

options.text: Information or references that span a chunk boundary (e.g., a term defined in one chunk and used in another) may not be properly connected without some overlap or summary linking the chunks
Chunking always preserves 100% of context automatically with no possible loss
This concern only applies to numerical data, never textual content
Context loss between chunks is never a real concern

questions.explanation: Cross-references and dependencies that span chunk boundaries can be lost without deliberate overlap or a linking summary between chunks.

questions.stem: A user notices that Claude's responses to similar requests keep following the exact same formulaic pattern. What is a practical fix?

options.text: Nothing can be done; formulaic output cannot be changed
Vary the prompt framing, provide a different reference example, or explicitly ask for a different structure/approach
Always accept the formulaic output regardless of fit
Switch to a completely unrelated task instead

questions.explanation: Deliberately varying framing, examples, or explicitly requesting a different approach are the direct levers for breaking a formulaic pattern.

questions.stem: A marketing team keeps getting similar-sounding taglines despite different product briefs. What change is most likely to help?

options.text: Continue submitting identical prompt structures indefinitely
Reduce the number of taglines requested to exactly one
Remove all product details from the prompt
Explicitly request a different creative approach, tone, or persona for each brief, rather than reusing a nearly identical prompt template each time

questions.explanation: Varying the creative framing/persona per request breaks the pattern of reusing a template that naturally produces similar-sounding results.

questions.stem: Why might using the same reference example repeatedly contribute to formulaic output over time?

options.text: Reference examples never influence subsequent output in any way
Reference examples always guarantee maximum variety with no downside
A single repeated reference example can anchor responses to its specific style/structure so consistently that genuine variation becomes less likely
This effect only occurs with numerical data, never text

questions.explanation: A consistently reused reference example can over-anchor output to its particular pattern, at the cost of genuine variety.

questions.stem: A user wants a set of five distinct, non-repetitive product descriptions. What is a useful strategy?

options.text: Ask for each description to highlight a different angle or benefit, or generate them with explicitly varied framing to avoid convergence on one pattern
Request all five in a single generic prompt with no differentiation between them
Provide no distinguishing guidance and hope for natural variety
Request only one description and copy it five times

questions.explanation: Explicitly assigning different angles or framings per item is a direct way to produce genuinely distinct outputs rather than near-duplicates.

questions.stem: What role can explicitly pointing out the repetitive pattern to Claude play in fixing it?

options.text: Pointing out patterns only works for numerical content
No role; Claude cannot adjust based on this kind of feedback
This feedback always makes the repetition worse
Explicitly naming the specific repetitive pattern observed gives Claude concrete information to consciously avoid repeating it in the next attempt

questions.explanation: Specific, named feedback about the observed pattern is exactly the kind of concrete signal that supports a genuinely different next attempt.

questions.stem: A response that was supposed to be a table instead comes back as unstructured, misaligned text. What is a direct fix?

options.text: Assume tables can never be produced correctly
Delete the request and never ask for tables again
Explicitly request the content be reformatted using proper table/Markdown syntax with clear column headers
Accept the misaligned text as-is with no changes

questions.explanation: Explicitly requesting proper table/Markdown formatting with clear headers is the direct fix for a misaligned or unstructured attempt at tabular output.

questions.stem: A user needs a response's formatting to match a very specific style used elsewhere in their organization. What is the most reliable fix if the first attempt doesn't match?

options.text: Accept the mismatch and manually reformat everything by hand every time
Provide a concrete example of the exact desired formatting style, and ask for the content to be reformatted to match it
Give up on requesting that formatting style ever again
Assume formatting requests are never possible to fulfill

questions.explanation: A concrete example of the target formatting style gives a clear, checkable target for the reformatted output to match.

questions.stem: Why might explicitly naming the desired formatting syntax (e.g., 'use Markdown table syntax with a header row') help resolve a formatting problem?

options.text: Syntax instructions only work for code-related outputs
This approach always makes formatting worse
Naming specific syntax never has any effect on output formatting
Explicit syntax instructions remove ambiguity about exactly what structure is wanted, increasing the odds of getting properly formatted output on the next attempt

questions.explanation: Precise syntax instructions reduce ambiguity, directly increasing the likelihood of correctly structured output.

questions.stem: A response includes inconsistent formatting (some items bulleted, others in paragraph form) within what should be a single consistent list. What is the appropriate fix?

options.text: Accept the inconsistency since the content itself is accurate
Ask for the entire list to be reformatted consistently as bullet points (or whichever single format is desired) throughout
Delete half the list to eliminate the inconsistency
Assume consistent formatting is not achievable

questions.explanation: A direct request to standardize the format throughout is the straightforward fix for inconsistent formatting within a single piece of content.

questions.stem: A user's specific request for a conversation seems to conflict with a standing Project-level custom instruction. What is a reasonable way to resolve this?

options.text: Ignore both instructions entirely and produce unrelated content
Delete the Project entirely any time a conflict arises
Assume conflicts of this kind can never occur
Recognize the conflict, and either clarify which should take precedence for this specific case or update the Project instruction if the standing default itself needs to change

questions.explanation: Explicitly recognizing and resolving the conflict — rather than ignoring it or overreacting — is the practical troubleshooting step.

questions.stem: A response doesn't follow an expected standing rule, and investigation reveals the rule was never actually saved as a Project instruction — it was only mentioned once in an old, separate conversation. What does this reveal?

options.text: This situation cannot actually occur
The AI system is fundamentally broken
A one-off mention in a past, separate conversation doesn't persist as a standing rule the way an actual saved Project instruction would — the fix is to properly configure it as a Project instruction
Standing rules are never possible to configure

questions.explanation: This is a configuration gap, not a malfunction — properly saving the rule as a Project instruction is the direct fix.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to audit for conflicting instructions periodically, especially as a Project's configuration grows more complex over time?

options.text: Audits are only relevant for extremely small Projects with almost no configuration
Complexity never leads to any configuration issues
Auditing is never useful and should be avoided
As more instructions accumulate, the chance of unnoticed contradictions between them increases, and periodic review helps catch and resolve these before they cause confusing or inconsistent output

questions.explanation: Growing configuration complexity increases the chance of unnoticed contradictions, making periodic review a practical maintenance habit.

questions.stem: Two different Project-level instructions unintentionally give contradictory guidance about desired response length. What is the appropriate fix?

options.text: Leave both contradictory instructions in place indefinitely
Review both instructions, determine the actually intended length preference, and update the Project configuration to remove the contradiction
Delete the entire Project and start over from nothing
Assume the contradiction will resolve itself automatically

questions.explanation: Directly reviewing and reconciling the contradictory instructions is the appropriate fix, rather than leaving them unresolved or over-reacting.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable practice to reduce the likelihood of conflicting instructions accumulating over time?

options.text: Periodically review the full set of standing instructions together for consistency, especially before adding significant new ones
Never update or add any instructions after the initial setup
Add new instructions indefinitely with no review of how they interact with existing ones
Conflicting instructions are impossible to prevent under any circumstances

questions.explanation: Reviewing the full set of instructions together — especially when adding new ones — helps catch conflicts before they accumulate unnoticed.

questions.stem: A weekly digest summarizing dozens of short internal updates needs to be produced quickly and cheaply, with only moderate nuance required. What tier consideration applies?

options.text: A faster, more lightweight tier is likely well-suited given the task's volume and moderate complexity
Only the most expensive tier can summarize text of any kind
Tier choice is irrelevant to a summarization task
The slowest available option should always be chosen for summaries

questions.explanation: Moderate-complexity, high-volume summarization is a good fit for a faster, lighter tier rather than defaulting to the most expensive option.

questions.stem: Why might it be worth periodically re-evaluating which model tier is used for a recurring business task?

options.text: Only the very first tier ever tried should be used indefinitely
Re-evaluation is never worthwhile once a tier is chosen
Task needs, available tiers, and cost/quality tradeoffs can evolve over time, so periodic re-evaluation helps ensure the chosen tier still fits current needs
Tier choice should be made once and never reconsidered under any circumstances

questions.explanation: As needs and available options change over time, periodically confirming the tier choice still fits is a reasonable practice rather than a one-time, permanent decision.

questions.stem: A user finds that a lightweight tier's output for a moderately complex task requires substantial manual correction each time. What does this suggest?

options.text: Manual correction needs are unrelated to model tier choice
The lightweight tier is always the correct choice regardless of correction needs
The task's actual complexity may exceed what the lightweight tier reliably handles, suggesting a more capable tier could reduce the correction burden
The user should stop attempting the task altogether

questions.explanation: Consistent, substantial correction needs are a practical signal that the chosen tier may be under-matched to the task's real complexity.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to test whether a faster/cheaper tier is sufficient for a new recurring task before fully committing to it?

options.text: Testing is never necessary or useful for this kind of decision
Assume sufficiency with no testing and commit immediately
Only test with a tier that is known to be insufficient
Run a small trial comparing the lighter tier's output quality against the task's actual requirements before rolling it out broadly

questions.explanation: A small-scale trial against real requirements is a practical, low-risk way to validate tier sufficiency before broader adoption.

questions.stem: Two tasks have identical output length requirements but very different reasoning complexity. Should they necessarily use the same model tier?

options.text: Not necessarily — reasoning complexity, not just output length, is a key factor, so the more complex task may warrant a more capable tier even with similar length needs
Yes, output length is the only factor that should determine tier choice
Both tasks should always use the least capable available tier regardless of complexity
Tier choice should never consider task complexity

questions.explanation: Complexity of reasoning required — not just how long the output is — is a primary driver of appropriate tier selection.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects a balanced view of model tier selection for business use?

options.text: Tier selection is purely about minimizing cost with no regard for output quality
Tier selection is purely about maximizing capability with no regard for cost or speed
Tier selection should balance the task's actual complexity/stakes against cost and speed considerations, rather than optimizing for only one factor in isolation
Tier selection has no meaningful tradeoffs to consider

questions.explanation: Sound tier selection weighs complexity/stakes against cost/speed together, rather than optimizing a single dimension in isolation.

questions.stem: A user wants to build a lightweight internal tool (like a simple form or calculator) they can hand off to colleagues to use directly. Which product surface fits best?

options.text: A Project with no artifact generated
A single emoji response
An artifact capable of rendering the actual interactive tool for colleagues to use
A plain text-only chat reply describing the tool conceptually

questions.explanation: A hands-on, usable tool for colleagues is best delivered as an interactive artifact rather than a conceptual text description.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a Claude Project from a single ordinary conversation?

options.text: A Project persists shared context, instructions, and knowledge sources across many related conversations, while an ordinary conversation is a single, standalone thread
Projects can only ever contain a single conversation, identical to an ordinary chat
There is no meaningful distinction between the two
Ordinary conversations always have access to more features than any Project

questions.explanation: The defining feature of a Project is persistence and sharing of context across multiple related conversations, unlike a standalone single conversation.

questions.stem: A user wants to keep a growing, evolving reference document that gets revised over many sessions. Which surface best fits this ongoing need?

options.text: An artifact that can be revisited and iteratively edited across sessions, potentially within a Project for added persistent context
A single, one-time inline reply with no further access
A brand-new, disconnected conversation each time with no continuity
Deleting the document after each session

questions.explanation: An evolving, editable reference is best supported by a persistent artifact, especially when paired with a Project for ongoing context.

questions.stem: Why does knowing which product surfaces are available matter for effective everyday use of Claude?

options.text: Product surfaces are irrelevant to task efficiency
Surface choice is determined entirely at random with no user influence
Choosing the surface that matches the task (ongoing project work, standalone reusable content, current information needs, or quick chat) leads to more efficient and effective use
It doesn't matter; all surfaces behave identically in every respect

questions.explanation: Matching surface to task need is a practical efficiency skill — the various surfaces exist because different tasks have genuinely different requirements.

questions.stem: A user is deciding whether a piece of work belongs in a Project or as a one-off conversation. Which question is most relevant?

options.text: How many words are in the first sentence of the request?
Is today a weekday?
What is the current outdoor temperature?
Will this work benefit from shared, persistent context across multiple future conversations?

questions.explanation: Whether the work will benefit from persistent, shared context across future conversations is the substantive question for choosing a Project versus a one-off chat.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable takeaway about combining product surfaces (e.g., using Artifacts within a Project)?

options.text: Only one single surface may ever be used across an entire organization
Using more than one surface at a time always causes errors
Product surfaces can never be combined or used together
Surfaces can complement each other — for example, a Project can provide persistent context while an artifact within it holds a specific reusable deliverable

questions.explanation: Product surfaces are often complementary rather than mutually exclusive, each serving a different aspect of the same body of work.

questions.stem: A user needs to verify a claim about very recent industry news as part of a broader request. Which feature addresses this specific need within the larger task?

options.text: A Project with outdated knowledge sources
Ignoring the need for current information entirely
A feature that retrieves current information from the web, used for that specific portion of the task
An artifact with no connection to current data

questions.explanation: Even within a larger task, the specific need for current information should be met with a current-information-retrieval feature rather than static knowledge alone.

questions.stem: Why might using the wrong feature for a task (e.g., plain chat for something needing persistent shared context) reduce efficiency over time?

options.text: Using the wrong feature always produces identical results to using the right one
Feature mismatch never has any efficiency impact
Without the right feature, users may end up manually re-doing work (like re-explaining context) that the appropriate feature would have handled automatically
All features are perfectly interchangeable with no efficiency differences

questions.explanation: Mismatched feature choice creates avoidable manual overhead that the correctly-matched feature would have eliminated.

questions.stem: A user needs both a quick answer right now AND wants to build persistent context for future related work. What is a reasonable approach?

options.text: Only ever address one of the two needs, never both
These two needs can never be reasonably combined
Answer the immediate question, and also consider setting up a Project going forward if this represents the start of an ongoing body of related work
Ignore the immediate question entirely in favor of Project setup

questions.explanation: Serving the immediate need while also recognizing the value of setting up persistent context for the future addresses both needs without compromising either.

questions.stem: What is a sound mental checklist question for choosing the right feature before starting a new piece of work?

options.text: Is this part of ongoing work that would benefit from persistent context, does it need current information, and will the output be a substantial reusable deliverable?
What color scheme does the user prefer?
How many people are in the building right now?
What was the very first thing the user ever asked Claude?

questions.explanation: These three questions — persistence, currency of information, and substance/reusability — map directly onto the decision points between Projects, search-enabled modes, and artifacts.

questions.stem: An organization scaling from a handful of users to hundreds wants consistent policy enforcement across everyone. What deployment consideration becomes more important at this scale?

options.text: Centralized administration and policy consistency become more valuable as the number of users and the coordination need grows
Scale has no bearing on which deployment approach makes sense
Individual, disconnected accounts always scale better than any centralized approach
Policy enforcement becomes irrelevant as an organization grows

questions.explanation: The value of centralized administration and consistent policy grows as coordination needs increase with organizational scale.

questions.stem: Why might data-handling policies differ between an individual personal account and an organization-managed deployment?

options.text: Personal accounts always have stricter data-handling policies than organizational ones
This distinction is never relevant to actual usage
Organization-managed deployments often include specific administrative controls and data-handling terms suited to business/compliance needs that individual accounts may not include
Data-handling policies are always identical regardless of account type

questions.explanation: Organization-level deployments are typically built with business/compliance-oriented administrative and data-handling features not present in individual personal accounts.

questions.stem: A small startup with three employees is evaluating whether an organization-level deployment is worth the added complexity compared to individual accounts. What is a reasonable consideration?

options.text: Organization-level deployment is always worth it regardless of team size or coordination needs
Individual accounts become illegal to use once a company has more than one employee
At a very small scale with minimal coordination needs, individual accounts might be sufficient for now, with a reassessment as the team and its governance needs grow
Team size should never factor into this kind of decision
