questions.explanation: Deployment choice can reasonably scale with actual coordination and governance needs, which are typically lower for a very small team.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable factor for an organization to weigh when choosing a plan/deployment tier?

options.text: A random selection with no evaluation criteria at all
Only the personal preference of a single employee with no regard for broader organizational needs
The specific combination of collaboration needs, required administrative controls, and expected usage volume across the organization
The plan chosen by an unrelated organization in a completely different industry, with no consideration of fit

questions.explanation: Weighing actual collaboration needs, administrative requirements, and usage volume is the substantive basis for a sound plan/deployment decision.

questions.stem: A user needs a quick answer to a factual question about a well-established, stable topic with no recency concerns. Which feature is most proportionate?

options.text: A research/current-information mode, even though no current data is actually needed
An artifact, regardless of the question's simplicity
Plain conversation relying on general knowledge, since no current-information retrieval or persistent project context is actually needed here
A full Project configured specifically for this single question

questions.explanation: When neither currency of information nor persistent context is actually needed, plain conversation is the simplest, most proportionate choice.

questions.stem: Why is it a mistake to default to the most feature-heavy option (e.g., always using a Project with a research mode and an artifact) regardless of the task?

options.text: Using more machinery than a task actually needs adds unnecessary setup overhead without a corresponding benefit, when a simpler approach would have worked just as well
This consideration is irrelevant to everyday productivity
It is never a mistake; maximum features should always be used for every task
Feature-heavy options always produce strictly worse results than simple ones in every case

questions.explanation: Matching feature intensity to actual task needs avoids unnecessary overhead — over-provisioning has a real efficiency cost even when it doesn't reduce quality.

questions.stem: Output needs to feed into an automated system that only accepts a specific structured field order. What is the most efficient workflow design?

options.text: Generate output in a convenient but mismatched format and manually reorder fields afterward every time
Ask the automated system to change its requirements to match whatever format is easiest to generate
Avoid integrating with the automated system entirely
Specify the exact required field order in the prompt itself, so the generated output can be fed into the system without manual reordering

questions.explanation: Specifying the destination's exact requirements up front avoids a recurring manual reordering step downstream.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable habit when designing a recurring workflow step that produces output for a specific downstream tool?

options.text: Never document or standardize the expected format; re-derive it from scratch every time
Document the downstream tool's format requirements once, and reuse that specification consistently every time the workflow step runs
Assume the downstream tool will adapt to whatever format is produced with no consideration needed
Change the required format randomly each time the workflow runs

questions.explanation: Documenting and reusing a consistent format specification avoids re-deriving requirements from scratch on every run of a recurring workflow step.

questions.stem: A workflow step's output will be read aloud in a meeting rather than displayed visually. What format consideration is most relevant?

options.text: Format is irrelevant if the content will be spoken rather than read
The output should be a single word regardless of content needs
Simpler, more linear prose suited to being read aloud, since visually-dependent formatting like tables doesn't translate well to spoken delivery
Dense tables and complex visual formatting, since these translate well to spoken delivery

questions.explanation: Matching format to how the output will actually be consumed — spoken delivery favors linear prose over visual structures like tables — avoids a mismatch.

questions.stem: Why might a workflow define format requirements separately for each distinct downstream consumer of the same underlying content?

options.text: Content should never be reused across more than one downstream consumer
All downstream consumers always require identical formatting with no exceptions
Defining requirements separately is always unnecessary extra work with no benefit
Different consumers (a spreadsheet import, a client email, a slide deck) may need the same underlying information presented in different structures

questions.explanation: The same underlying content often needs different structural treatment depending on where it's actually going next.

questions.stem: A team wants the same underlying analysis delivered both as a detailed internal document and as a short external-facing summary. What is a sound approach?

options.text: Refuse to produce more than one version of any analysis
Always default to the least detailed version for both audiences
Generate two format/detail-appropriate versions from the same underlying analysis — one detailed for internal use, one condensed for external use
Produce only one version and force it to serve both purposes without adaptation

questions.explanation: Producing purpose-appropriate versions from the same underlying analysis serves both audiences properly, rather than forcing one format to fit two different needs.

questions.stem: A user is about to start a new phase of a multi-month project and wants the new conversation to have the essential background without an overwhelming amount of historical detail. What is a reasonable approach?

options.text: Prepare a concise summary of the essential decisions and context, and use that as the starting point for the new conversation
Paste the entire multi-month conversation history verbatim into the new conversation
Start with absolutely no context and hope it works out
Refuse to start a new conversation and continue the original indefinitely regardless of length

questions.explanation: A concise, curated summary gives the new conversation what it actually needs without the overhead of the full historical record.

questions.stem: What is a tradeoff to consider when deciding whether to persist context via a Project versus re-supplying it manually each time?

options.text: Persisting via a Project reduces repetitive manual work for recurring needs, but requires the upfront effort of setting it up and keeping it current — a worthwhile tradeoff for genuinely recurring work
There is no tradeoff; persisting context is always strictly better with no consideration needed
Manual re-supply is always more efficient than any form of persistence
This tradeoff only applies to coding-related work

questions.explanation: Persistence trades upfront setup/maintenance effort for reduced repetitive work — a good trade specifically when the context is genuinely reused across many future instances.

questions.stem: A user notices that a very long conversation is starting to reference earlier points inconsistently. What is a reasonable interpretation and next step?

options.text: This is unrelated to conversation length and requires no action
This may be a sign the conversation has grown long enough that a summarized restart would help restore focus and consistency
The user should immediately abandon the entire project
Inconsistency at this stage should always be ignored

questions.explanation: Growing inconsistency in a very long conversation is a practical signal that summarizing and restarting may help restore focus.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to distinguish between context that is truly one-off versus context that will be needed repeatedly across future conversations?

options.text: This distinction is never useful for managing context effectively
All context should always be persisted regardless of whether it recurs
Recognizing recurring context supports a decision to persist it (e.g., via a Project), while one-off context is reasonably handled with a manual, single-use mention
All context should never be persisted under any circumstances

questions.explanation: Distinguishing recurring from one-off context is what informs a sensible decision about whether persistence effort is actually worthwhile.

questions.stem: A company wants to integrate Claude into its customer feedback analysis process, which currently ends with a human analyst writing a summary report by hand. What is a sound integration point?

options.text: Have Claude fully replace the analyst with no human review of the final report
Avoid integrating Claude into this process at all
Have Claude randomly alter the existing process with no clear purpose
Have Claude assist the analyst by organizing and drafting an initial summary from the raw feedback, with the analyst reviewing, refining, and taking ownership of the final report

questions.explanation: Assisting the existing analyst's drafting work — while preserving their review and ownership of the final output — is a sound, targeted integration.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to communicate a new AI-assisted step to the people who work within an existing business process?

options.text: Communication is never necessary for process changes
Change the process silently with no communication to those involved
Only communicate the change to people outside the process
Clearly explain what has changed, what AI assistance now handles, and what remains a human responsibility, so everyone understands the new process

questions.explanation: Clear communication about what changed and where responsibilities now sit helps a new AI-assisted step actually function well within an existing team process.

questions.stem: After integrating Claude into a process step, employees report the new step is actually slower than the original manual approach for certain edge cases. What is a reasonable response?

options.text: Ignore the feedback and assume the integration is always correct as originally designed
Blame the employees for the slower performance with no further investigation
Investigate the specific edge cases, and adjust the integration (e.g., route those cases back to the original manual approach) if AI assistance genuinely isn't adding value there
Immediately discontinue all AI assistance across the entire organization

questions.explanation: Targeted investigation and adjustment for the specific cases where integration isn't helping is a more proportionate response than blanket dismissal or blanket abandonment.

questions.stem: A workflow chains: gather requirements, draft a proposal, internal review, client review, finalize. Where is a particularly important checkpoint to get right, and why?

options.text: Before the client review stage, since catching issues internally first avoids exposing unpolished or incorrect content to the client
Only after the client has already seen and reacted to the proposal
There are no important checkpoints; all stages are equally trivial
The order of these stages has no bearing on the outcome

questions.explanation: Catching problems during internal review — before external/client exposure — protects the client relationship and avoids a more costly correction later.

questions.stem: What is a benefit of explicitly naming each stage of a multi-step workflow (rather than leaving the process implicit)?

options.text: Explicit stages always slow down a process with no benefit
Implicit, undocumented processes are always more efficient than explicit ones
Naming stages has no practical benefit
Explicit stages make it easier for everyone involved to know what's expected at each point, and make it clearer where a checkpoint or handoff should occur

questions.explanation: Clarity about each stage's role supports better coordination and makes checkpoint placement more deliberate rather than accidental.

questions.stem: A multi-step workflow currently has a review checkpoint after every single minor sub-step, causing significant delays. What adjustment reflects sound workflow design?

options.text: Add even more checkpoints to every remaining sub-step
Remove every checkpoint entirely, including ones at genuinely critical transitions
Leave the workflow entirely unchanged despite the delays
Consolidate or remove checkpoints for low-stakes sub-steps while preserving them at genuinely critical transitions where catching an error matters most

questions.explanation: Trimming checkpoints proportional to actual risk — rather than removing them all or leaving excessive checkpoints everywhere — balances speed and safety.

questions.stem: A user is setting up a new Project for a recurring type of client work. Which is a reasonable first step?

options.text: Configure settings entirely unrelated to the actual client work
Skip any configuration and treat every conversation as a fresh, unconfigured start
Immediately delete the Project after creating it
Define the standing custom instructions (tone, format, recurring context) and identify the knowledge sources that should be available across this Project's conversations

questions.explanation: Establishing standing instructions and relevant knowledge sources up front is the foundational setup step for a Project meant to support recurring work.

questions.stem: What is a practical benefit of writing Project custom instructions with the same clarity principles used for individual prompts?

options.text: Clarity only matters for the very first conversation in a Project
Vague Project instructions always work just as well as clear ones
Since Project instructions apply automatically across many future conversations, clarity at setup time has an outsized, compounding benefit compared to a single one-off prompt
There is no benefit; Project instructions and individual prompts follow entirely different principles

questions.explanation: Because Project instructions apply broadly and repeatedly, getting them right at setup time pays off across every future conversation in that Project.

questions.stem: A Project's custom instructions are so long and unfocused that they seem to produce inconsistent results. What is a reasonable fix?

options.text: Add even more instructions to the already-long set with no editing
Review and streamline the instructions to focus on the genuinely important, consistent standing guidance, removing redundant or unclear parts
Delete the Project entirely with no attempt to fix the instructions
Assume instruction length never affects consistency

questions.explanation: Streamlining overly long or unfocused instructions to their genuinely important core tends to improve consistency more than adding further length.

questions.stem: Why might a Project dedicated to a single, well-defined recurring task (e.g., weekly report generation) benefit especially strongly from custom instructions?

options.text: A narrowly-scoped, recurring task has stable, predictable requirements that are especially well captured by a consistent set of standing instructions
Single-purpose Projects never benefit from any custom instructions
Narrowly-scoped Projects should avoid any configuration entirely
Custom instructions only provide value for Projects covering many unrelated tasks

questions.explanation: Stable, predictable, recurring requirements are exactly what standing custom instructions are best suited to capture and enforce consistently.

questions.stem: A team lead wants new team members to quickly get up to speed on how a shared Project is configured. What is a reasonable practice?

options.text: Expect new members to guess the configuration through trial and error with no guidance
Maintain a brief, current written overview of the Project's instructions and knowledge sources for new team members to reference
Avoid onboarding new members to shared Projects entirely
Reconfigure the entire Project from scratch every time a new member joins

questions.explanation: A current, accessible overview of the Project's setup helps new team members use it correctly without unnecessary trial and error.

questions.stem: What is a sound approach if a Project's purpose changes significantly over time (e.g., shifting from one client to a different one)?

options.text: Leave all original configuration in place with no changes despite the shift
Review and update the Project's custom instructions and knowledge sources to reflect the new purpose, rather than leaving outdated configuration in place
Immediately delete the Project with no reconfiguration option considered
Assume the original configuration will automatically adapt to the new purpose with no changes needed

questions.explanation: A significant shift in purpose calls for a deliberate configuration review and update, rather than leaving stale settings in place.

questions.stem: A user wants a Project's custom instructions to specify both a required tone AND a required structure for all outputs. Is this a reasonable use of custom instructions?

options.text: Yes, but only if the two requirements are contradictory
No; custom instructions can only specify one type of guidance at a time
Yes; custom instructions can reasonably capture multiple standing requirements (tone, structure, and more) as long as they're expressed clearly
No; tone and structure can never both be controlled through Project configuration

questions.explanation: Custom instructions can reasonably combine multiple clear, complementary standing requirements like tone and structure together.

questions.stem: Why might it be useful to include a brief statement of PURPOSE (not just rules) in a Project's custom instructions?

options.text: Understanding the underlying purpose can help produce better judgment calls in situations the specific rules don't explicitly cover
Purpose statements are never useful in custom instructions
Purpose statements should always replace specific rules entirely
Purpose has no bearing on how instructions are followed

questions.explanation: A stated purpose gives useful context for handling edge cases the specific rules don't explicitly anticipate.

questions.stem: A Project is configured for internal use only, but a user is considering sharing some of its generated content externally. What should this prompt the user to reconsider?

options.text: External sharing decisions are entirely unrelated to how a Project was configured
Nothing; internal configuration is always safe to share externally with no changes
The Project should be deleted immediately due to this consideration

Whether the content's tone, detail level, or included information (calibrated for an internal audience) is actually appropriate for external distribution, since the Project was configured with internal use in mind

questions.explanation: Content calibrated for an internal-audience Project may need review before external distribution, since the original configuration wasn't designed with that audience in mind.

questions.stem: A Project includes several overlapping reference documents that occasionally contradict each other on small details. What risk does this create?

options.text: Responses may inconsistently draw from whichever conflicting detail happens to be referenced, so reconciling or clarifying which source is authoritative is worthwhile
This situation is not possible in practice
No risk; contradictions between knowledge sources never affect responses
Contradictions should be resolved by deleting all knowledge sources from the Project

questions.explanation: Overlapping, contradictory knowledge sources can lead to inconsistent grounding — reconciling which source is authoritative addresses the actual risk.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable check to perform after adding a new knowledge source to an existing Project?

options.text: Assume the new source will conflict with everything else in the Project
Immediately remove the knowledge source without ever testing it
No check is necessary; new knowledge sources always integrate perfectly with no verification
Test that responses in that Project appropriately draw on the newly added material where relevant, confirming the configuration worked as intended

questions.explanation: A quick verification that the new material is actually being used appropriately confirms the configuration is working as intended.

questions.stem: A Project's knowledge sources include a document with clearly sensitive information not needed for the Project's actual purpose. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Remove the unnecessary sensitive document, since including sensitive material not actually needed for the Project's purpose is an avoidable exposure
Add even more unrelated sensitive documents alongside it
Leave the unnecessary sensitive document in place since removing it might be inconvenient
Ignore the mismatch since knowledge sources are never a privacy consideration

questions.explanation: Removing unnecessary sensitive material that doesn't serve the Project's actual purpose reduces avoidable exposure — a straightforward data-minimization practice.

questions.stem: Why might it be useful to periodically audit which knowledge sources are actually being used effectively within a Project?

options.text: Over time, some sources may become outdated, redundant, or irrelevant, and periodic review helps keep the Project's knowledge base accurate and appropriately scoped
This kind of audit is only relevant for extremely large Projects
Knowledge sources never need review once configured
Auditing knowledge sources is never useful once they've been added

questions.explanation: Periodic review catches drift toward outdated or irrelevant material, keeping the knowledge base genuinely useful over time.

questions.stem: A user wants a Project to reference a document that updates frequently outside of Claude (e.g., a live spreadsheet). What consideration is most relevant?

options.text: This consideration only applies to non-business Projects
Live, frequently-updating documents should never be used as knowledge sources under any circumstances
No consideration is needed; the knowledge source will always automatically reflect the very latest live version with no user action
Understanding how and when the uploaded reference material needs to be refreshed to stay reasonably current, since a one-time upload reflects only a snapshot

questions.explanation: A knowledge source added as an upload is a snapshot at that point in time — understanding the need to refresh it is important for a frequently-changing source.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable principle for scoping which documents belong in a given Project's knowledge sources?

options.text: Include as many documents as possible from across the entire organization regardless of relevance
Include no documents at all under any circumstances
Scoping should be based purely on document file size
Include documents that are genuinely relevant to that Project's specific purpose, keeping the knowledge base focused rather than diluted with unrelated material

questions.explanation: Relevance to the Project's actual purpose — not sheer volume or file size — is the sound basis for scoping knowledge sources.

questions.stem: A user adds a knowledge source containing outdated contact information for a partner organization. Later, responses reference this outdated contact. What is the root cause and fix?

options.text: The outdated knowledge source is the root cause; updating or removing it is the direct fix to prevent further outdated references
This is not fixable under any circumstances
The issue can only be fixed by deleting the entire Project
The root cause is unrelated to the knowledge source; no fix related to it is needed

questions.explanation: Tracing the outdated reference back to its source material and updating or removing that source is the direct, appropriate fix.

questions.stem: Why is scoping knowledge sources tightly to a Project's purpose generally preferable to adding broad, loosely-related material 'just in case'?

options.text: Broad, loosely-related material always improves response quality with no downside
Scoping considerations are irrelevant to response quality
'Just in case' inclusion is always the best default strategy
Tightly-scoped, relevant sources reduce the risk of irrelevant or contradictory material diluting or confusing responses, and reduce unnecessary exposure of unrelated content

questions.explanation: Focused knowledge sources reduce dilution/contradiction risk and avoid unnecessarily exposing unrelated content within that Project's context.

questions.stem: A user wants a one-time exception to a Project's standing formatting rule for a single specific request. What is the appropriate way to express this?

options.text: Permanently delete the Project's standing formatting rule to accommodate the one-time exception
Explicitly state the desired exception for that specific request, understanding it applies to this instance without needing to change the underlying standing rule
Assume exceptions are never possible and abandon the request
Create an entirely new Project just for this one exception

questions.explanation: A clearly stated, request-specific exception is the proportionate way to handle a one-off deviation without altering the standing default.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to think about the relationship between a Project's standing instructions and a specific in-conversation request?

options.text: The standing instructions and specific requests can never coexist or interact in any way
Specific requests are always completely ignored in favor of standing instructions with no exception

The standing instructions provide a consistent default, while a specific request can reasonably adjust behavior for that instance, similar to how a general policy can allow for specific, stated exceptions
Standing instructions are always completely ignored in favor of the most recent specific request

questions.explanation: This relationship mirrors general-policy-with-specific-exception reasoning: a sensible default that can flex for an explicitly stated, specific case.

questions.stem: A user is troubleshooting why a Project seems to apply a rule inconsistently across different conversations. What is a good diagnostic step?

options.text: Assume the inconsistency is unexplainable and cannot be investigated
Assume all conversations within a Project always behave identically regardless of configuration
Check whether the rule was actually set at the Project level (applying to all conversations) versus having only been mentioned in one specific past conversation
Delete the Project immediately with no further diagnosis

questions.explanation: Confirming the actual scope where a rule was set (Project-wide vs. one conversation) is the direct way to diagnose apparent inconsistency.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to think of Project-level instructions as 'defaults' rather than absolute, unchangeable rules?

options.text: Defaults and absolute rules are identical concepts with no meaningful difference
This framing implies Project instructions have no effect at all
Thinking of them as defaults captures how they provide consistent baseline behavior while still reasonably accommodating specific, explicitly stated exceptions for individual requests
This framing is inaccurate and should never be used

questions.explanation: The 'default' framing captures the practical reality: consistent baseline behavior that can still flex for a clearly stated specific case.

questions.stem: A user wants to permanently change a Project's standing behavior, not just make a one-time exception. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Update the actual Project-level custom instructions, since that is the mechanism for changing standing, persistent behavior going forward
Create a brand new, entirely separate account to achieve this change
State the change only within a single conversation and expect it to permanently alter the Project's standing configuration
Permanent changes to standing behavior are not possible under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A genuinely permanent change to standing behavior requires updating the Project-level instructions themselves, not just a one-off in-conversation statement.

questions.stem: A team has grown from a single small group into several distinct sub-teams with different clients. What organizational adjustment is likely warranted?

options.text: Continue using exactly one shared Project for all sub-teams and all clients indefinitely with no changes
Merge every sub-team's work into a single conversation with no Project structure at all
Consider splitting into separate Projects aligned with each sub-team/client's distinct context, instructions, and knowledge sources
Eliminate all Projects and revert to entirely unconfigured conversations

questions.explanation: As distinct contexts emerge across sub-teams/clients, splitting into appropriately scoped separate Projects better serves each group's specific needs.

questions.stem: What is a risk of having too many overlapping, redundant Projects covering nearly the same work?

options.text: Redundant Projects can lead to inconsistent configuration (different instructions/knowledge sources for what should be the same context) and confusion about which Project to use
This scenario is not possible to create
There is no risk; more Projects are always better regardless of overlap
Overlapping Projects always automatically merge with no issue

questions.explanation: Redundant, overlapping Projects risk inconsistent configuration and confusion about where a given piece of work should actually happen.

questions.stem: A newly formed cross-functional team needs a shared space with consistent context for a specific initiative involving multiple departments. What is a reasonable setup?

options.text: Have each department maintain entirely separate, disconnected configurations with no shared context
Set up a single shared Project for the initiative, configured with the context and knowledge sources relevant to the cross-functional work
Avoid setting up any shared configuration since the team is cross-functional
Require each individual to memorize the initiative's context with no configured support

questions.explanation: A single shared Project tailored to the initiative gives the cross-functional team the consistent context it needs.

questions.stem: Why might assigning clear ownership for maintaining a shared team Project's configuration be a good practice?

options.text: Ownership is irrelevant; shared Projects maintain themselves automatically
Assigning ownership always makes shared Projects worse
Only individual, non-shared Projects can have an owner
Without clear ownership, a shared Project's instructions and knowledge sources may drift out of date with no one responsible for keeping them current

questions.explanation: Clear ownership ensures someone is actually responsible for keeping a shared Project's configuration accurate and current over time.

questions.stem: A user needs Claude's help drafting a document that references a real, specific dollar amount from an unreleased financial figure. What is a privacy-conscious approach if the exact figure isn't essential for the drafting task?

options.text: Always include the exact real figure regardless of necessity
Consider using a placeholder or rounded illustrative figure for drafting purposes if the exact real number isn't actually needed to complete the task
Refuse to draft any document that could ever involve financial figures
Share as many additional unreleased figures as possible for context

questions.explanation: Using a placeholder when the exact sensitive figure isn't actually necessary for the task is a practical data-minimization step.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable relationship between data sensitivity and the level of caution applied before sharing it in any tool, including Claude?

options.text: More sensitive data (financial, health, personal identifiers, confidential business information) warrants proportionally more caution and scrutiny of applicable policy before sharing
Caution should decrease as sensitivity increases
Sensitivity has no bearing on how data should be handled
All data should be treated with identical caution regardless of sensitivity

questions.explanation: Proportional caution — more scrutiny for more sensitive categories — is the sound, risk-based approach to data handling.

questions.stem: An employee is unsure whether a specific internal document counts as 'confidential' under their organization's policy. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Check the organization's classification policy or ask an appropriate contact to confirm the document's sensitivity level before sharing it
Assume all documents are always confidential and never use Claude for any related work
Assume it is not confidential and share it freely with no verification
Make a private guess with no reference to any organizational standard

questions.explanation: Verifying against the actual organizational classification (or asking) is more reliable than assuming or guessing about a document's sensitivity.

questions.stem: Why might anonymizing or redacting identifying details be a reasonable practice when the specific identity isn't necessary for a task?

options.text: Anonymizing details is never useful for any task involving sensitive data
This practice is only relevant to government organizations
Anonymizing details always makes tasks impossible to complete
It reduces exposure of unnecessary personal or confidential information while still allowing the underlying task to be completed effectively

questions.explanation: Removing unnecessary identifying detail is a practical way to reduce exposure while still getting the actual task done.

questions.stem: A user is drafting internal training material and wants to use a realistic example involving customer data. What is a privacy-conscious approach?

options.text: Use a fictional or clearly anonymized example that illustrates the same point without exposing real customer information
Use real customer data but only share it with a few colleagues
Use real, actual customer data taken directly from live records
Avoid creating any training materials that involve examples

questions.explanation: A fictional or anonymized example serves the training purpose just as well without exposing actual customer data.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable default when a task could be completed either with real sensitive data or an anonymized/synthetic equivalent?

options.text: Always default to using the real sensitive data for maximum realism regardless of necessity
Prefer the anonymized/synthetic equivalent when it serves the task's actual purpose just as well, minimizing unnecessary exposure of real sensitive data
The choice between the two options never matters from a privacy perspective
Synthetic data should never be used under any circumstances

questions.explanation: Preferring anonymized/synthetic data when it serves the purpose equally well is a sound, low-cost privacy practice.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to draft public-facing statements about a sensitive company event. What responsible-use consideration is most relevant?

options.text: No consideration is needed since drafting is just a starting point
Careful human review for accuracy, tone, and appropriateness before any public-facing statement is released, given the reputational and factual stakes involved
Public statements should always be sent exactly as first drafted
This scenario has no meaningful responsible-use considerations

questions.explanation: Public-facing, reputationally significant statements warrant careful human review before release, regardless of how the draft was produced.

questions.stem: Why is 'verify before relying on' a central theme across many responsible AI use principles?

options.text: Because AI-generated content can be fluent yet inaccurate or inappropriate, verification is the practical safeguard that lets people benefit from AI assistance while managing its risks
Verification is never actually necessary in practice
Verification only matters for creative writing tasks
This theme applies only to technical, coding-related use cases

questions.explanation: Verification is the practical bridge between AI's genuine usefulness and the real risk that fluent output can still be wrong or inappropriate.

questions.stem: An employee wants to use Claude to help draft feedback for a colleague's performance review. What is a responsible approach?

options.text: Send the AI-drafted feedback directly with no personal review or judgment applied
Avoid providing any personal input to feedback under any circumstances
Use the draft as a starting point, then apply personal judgment and direct knowledge of the colleague's actual performance before finalizing the feedback
Responsible use principles don't apply to performance feedback

questions.explanation: Personal judgment and direct knowledge should still shape and validate AI-assisted feedback before it's finalized, given its impact on a real person.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to think about the balance between efficiency gains from AI assistance and responsible use?

options.text: Efficiency should always be sacrificed entirely in favor of responsible use, with no middle ground
Efficiency and responsible use are always in complete conflict with no way to balance them
Responsible use principles should always be abandoned in favor of maximum efficiency

AI assistance can provide real efficiency gains while responsible practices (verification, appropriate review, privacy awareness) manage the accompanying risks — the two can coexist with thoughtful workflow design

questions.explanation: Thoughtful workflow design lets efficiency gains and responsible-use safeguards coexist, rather than treating them as strictly opposed.

questions.stem: A user is drafting content that will influence a decision about resource allocation between departments. What responsible-use consideration applies?

options.text: Given the potential for this content to meaningfully influence a consequential internal decision, applying appropriate scrutiny and verification before it's used is warranted
Only content shared externally ever requires responsible-use consideration
None; resource-allocation content requires no particular care
This type of content should never involve any AI assistance

questions.explanation: Content that meaningfully influences a consequential decision — even an internal one — warrants proportional scrutiny before being relied upon.

questions.stem: While drafting a response to a customer, a user notices language suggesting the customer may be in personal crisis. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Escalate to the appropriate internal process or trained personnel for handling sensitive personal situations, rather than treating it as a routine drafting task
Have Claude draft a purely transactional response and send it with no further consideration
Ignore the concerning language entirely since it's outside the scope of the original request
Ask Claude to resolve the personal crisis directly with no human involvement

questions.explanation: Signs of a potential personal crisis call for escalation to appropriate trained personnel or processes, not a purely transactional AI-drafted response.

questions.stem: Why might repeated, unexplained errors in an AI-assisted process be a signal for escalation beyond just fixing the immediate error?

options.text: Repeated errors are never worth escalating beyond the immediate fix
A persistent pattern of errors may indicate a deeper issue with how the process or tool is being used, which is worth surfacing to someone who can address the root cause
Repeated errors should always be resolved by simply ignoring them
This pattern has no bearing on whether escalation is warranted

questions.explanation: A persistent error pattern is a signal worth escalating beyond a one-off fix, since it may point to a systemic issue needing broader attention.

questions.stem: A user is asked to use Claude to help with a task that seems to conflict with a stated organizational value or policy. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Raise the apparent conflict with an appropriate person (e.g., a manager or compliance contact) before proceeding, rather than resolving the tension unilaterally
Refuse all future work indefinitely without raising the specific concern to anyone
Assume the conflict doesn't matter since AI is involved
Proceed with the task regardless of the apparent conflict

questions.explanation: Surfacing an apparent policy conflict to the appropriate person — rather than resolving it unilaterally or ignoring it — is the responsible escalation path.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to build organizational awareness of when escalation is appropriate for AI-assisted work?

options.text: Assume all employees will intuitively know when to escalate with no guidance provided
Provide clear examples and criteria (e.g., legal, safety, compliance, or significant consequence scenarios) as part of training and policy, so escalation triggers are well understood
Escalation criteria should be kept intentionally vague to avoid over-escalation
Escalation guidance is unnecessary since AI-assisted work never requires it

questions.explanation: Concrete examples and clear criteria in training/policy help build shared, consistent understanding of when escalation is actually warranted.

questions.stem: A document will be used only for internal brainstorming with no external distribution and no decision directly resting on it. How should this generally be categorized?

options.text: Medium-high risk regardless of audience or actual use
Risk category cannot be assessed for brainstorming documents under any circumstances
High risk, equivalent to an external regulatory filing
Generally lower risk, given the limited audience and lack of direct consequential decision resting on it — though this can change if its use later expands

questions.explanation: Limited audience and lack of direct consequential reliance are exactly the factors that generally place content in a lower risk category — though that categorization should be revisited if its use expands.

questions.stem: Why is risk categorization better understood as an ongoing assessment rather than a one-time label applied at creation?

options.text: The same content's actual risk can change as its intended use, audience, or distribution changes over time, so re-assessment may be warranted
Risk categorization should always be a permanent, one-time label with no reconsideration
Only the original creator's assessment ever matters, regardless of how the content is later used
Risk categorization is entirely arbitrary and provides no ongoing value

questions.explanation: Because actual risk depends on evolving use and audience, treating categorization as an ongoing check (not a permanent one-time label) is more accurate.

questions.stem: A piece of content was originally created for internal use (low risk) but is now being considered for external publication. What should happen?

options.text: Re-assess the content's risk category in light of the new external audience and apply the level of review appropriate to that higher-stakes context before publishing
External publication requires no additional scrutiny beyond the original internal review
Publish it externally with no reassessment, since it was already reviewed once for internal use
Risk category never needs to be reconsidered once content has been created

questions.explanation: A meaningful change in audience/use (internal to external) warrants re-categorizing risk and applying appropriately elevated review before publication.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to handle content that is genuinely ambiguous between two risk categories (e.g., between low and medium risk)?

options.text: Always default to treating ambiguous content as the lowest possible risk to save time
When genuinely ambiguous, erring toward the higher of the two plausible categories is a reasonably safe default, applying somewhat more review than might strictly be necessary
Ambiguous content should never be assessed at all
Ambiguity should be resolved by flipping a coin with no further judgment

questions.explanation: Given the asymmetric cost of under-reviewing higher-stakes content, erring toward the higher plausible category is a reasonably safe default in genuinely ambiguous cases.

questions.stem: An employee working across two different client accounts wonders if the same AI usage rules apply identically to both. What is a reasonable check?

options.text: Ignore client-specific considerations entirely
Assume no organizational policy could ever vary by client
Check whether either client relationship carries specific contractual or regulatory requirements that might mean different rules apply for each account
Assume identical rules apply to all clients with no verification

questions.explanation: Client-specific contractual or regulatory requirements can mean different rules genuinely apply per account, making a specific check worthwhile.

questions.stem: Why might an organization's AI policy explicitly list prohibited use cases in addition to approved ones?

options.text: Only approved-use lists are ever useful; prohibited-use lists are redundant
Prohibited-use lists serve no practical purpose
Prohibited-use lists are only relevant to non-AI tools
Explicitly naming known problematic use cases (e.g., certain high-risk or regulated activities) provides clear guardrails alongside the guidance on approved uses

questions.explanation: Explicit prohibited-use guidance provides clear guardrails for known problem areas, complementing guidance on what's approved.

questions.stem: A user repeatedly hits truncation on the same type of large recurring request. What is a more durable fix than repeatedly asking to 'continue' each time?

options.text: Restructure the recurring request into smaller, planned sections from the outset, so truncation is avoided proactively rather than fixed reactively each time
Continue tolerating repeated manual 'continue' requests indefinitely with no process change
Randomly change the topic of the request each time
Stop making this type of request altogether

questions.explanation: Proactively restructuring a recurring large request into planned sections is a more durable fix than repeatedly reacting to truncation after the fact.

questions.stem: What is a practical sign that a task should be planned in sections from the start, rather than attempted as one large request?

options.text: Past experience or the nature of the request suggests the full desired output is likely to be very long relative to typical response length
The task is very short and simple
The task has no relationship to length considerations
The request involves fewer than ten words

questions.explanation: Anticipating a very long output based on the nature or past experience of similar requests is the practical cue for proactive sectioning.

questions.stem: After receiving a continued response following truncation, a user notices a sentence appears to be duplicated across the boundary. What is the appropriate fix?

options.text: Discard the entire response and start over from nothing
Leave the duplication in place since it's a minor issue
Assume duplication at boundaries can never be fixed
Edit out the duplicated content at the boundary so the combined text reads as a single coherent passage

questions.explanation: A quick manual edit at the boundary is a proportionate fix for the occasional duplication that can occur when stitching together a continued response.

questions.stem: Why is recognizing truncation (versus assuming a response is simply complete) an important troubleshooting skill?

options.text: This skill is only relevant for very technical tasks
Recognizing truncation has no practical consequence either way
A trailing incomplete sentence or cut-off list can be mistaken for a complete response if not specifically checked for, leading to an unknowingly incomplete deliverable
Truncation is always obvious and requires no particular skill to recognize

questions.explanation: An unnoticed truncated response risks being used as if it were complete, so recognizing the signs is a practically important check.

questions.stem: A user needs to compare information from the beginning and end of a very large document that had to be chunked separately. What is a reasonable approach?

options.text: Combine the chunks back into their original unchunked form with no analysis
Only ever look at the first chunk and ignore the rest entirely
Assume the comparison is impossible once the document has been chunked
Extract the relevant specific details from each relevant chunk's analysis and explicitly compare them in a follow-up synthesis step

questions.explanation: A dedicated synthesis step that explicitly pulls together relevant details from different chunks is the practical way to make cross-chunk comparisons.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to decide how large each chunk of a document should be when splitting it for processing?

options.text: Chunk size is irrelevant and can be chosen completely at random
Always use exactly the same fixed chunk size regardless of the document's actual structure
Balance chunk size against practical processing limits and the need to preserve coherent, meaningful sections rather than splitting arbitrarily
Always split into the smallest possible chunks regardless of content

questions.explanation: Balancing practical size limits against preserving coherent sections is the sound basis for choosing chunk boundaries.

questions.stem: A user chunks a long contract into sections by page number, splitting some clauses mid-sentence across chunk boundaries. What problem does this risk creating?

options.text: No problem; page-based splitting is always the most reliable method
A clause split mid-sentence across chunks may be misinterpreted or evaluated incompletely within a single chunk, since a chunk-level analysis wouldn't see the clause's full text together
This approach guarantees a more accurate analysis than splitting by logical section
Contracts can never be meaningfully chunked under any method

questions.explanation: Splitting by an arbitrary boundary like page number, rather than logical structure like clauses, risks breaking up meaningful units of text mid-analysis.

questions.stem: Why might it help to briefly restate key relevant context from a previous chunk when processing the next chunk in sequence?

options.text: This technique is only relevant for numerical documents
This is never helpful and always wastes effort
Restating context always introduces new errors with no benefit
It gives the next chunk's processing step some continuity with what came before, reducing the risk of losing important cross-chunk connections

questions.explanation: Brief continuity context bridges the gap between chunks, helping preserve connections that a strict, isolated chunk-by-chunk approach might otherwise lose.

questions.stem: A user has tried varying the prompt wording several times but keeps getting essentially the same structure back. What is another lever to try?

options.text: Reduce the request to a single word with no further detail
Repeat the exact same wording one more time and expect a different result
Try a substantially different framing altogether — such as a different persona, a constraint that forces a new angle, or breaking the request into a different sequence of sub-steps
Give up on achieving variation entirely

questions.explanation: When minor wording tweaks aren't enough, a more substantial change in framing, persona, or constraints is the next lever to try for genuine variation.

questions.stem: Why might explicitly forbidding a specific overused phrase or structure help reduce formulaic output?

options.text: This technique never has any effect on output
Directly ruling out the specific pattern that's been recurring removes the 'default' option, pushing toward a genuinely different response
Forbidding phrases always makes output worse with no benefit
This technique only works for numerical content

questions.explanation: Explicitly ruling out the recurring pattern removes the path of least resistance, encouraging a genuinely different response.

questions.stem: A user wants Claude to avoid the very common opening structure of yet another business email starting with 'I hope this email finds you well.' What is a direct fix?

options.text: Accept the repeated opening as unavoidable
Explicitly instruct Claude to skip that specific stock opening and start with something more direct or specific to the situation
Rewrite only the closing while leaving the flagged opening untouched
Assume no instruction can influence this specific pattern

questions.explanation: Directly naming the specific pattern to avoid is the most reliable lever for eliminating it, especially for well-known, extremely common stock phrasings.

questions.stem: A user needs headers in a document to follow a specific numbering convention (e.g., 1.1, 1.2, 2.1) that the first draft didn't use. What is the direct fix?

options.text: Explicitly request the specific numbering convention needed, giving a short example if helpful, and ask for the headers to be reformatted accordingly
Accept the draft's existing header style with no changes
Assume numbering conventions can never be applied to headers
Remove all headers from the document entirely

questions.explanation: Explicitly specifying the exact convention (with an example if useful) is the direct way to get headers reformatted to match a specific numbering style.

questions.stem: Why can showing a small example of the exact desired formatting be more effective than describing it only in words?

options.text: Examples are never more effective than word descriptions for formatting
There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches for formatting
Examples can only be used for content, never for formatting
A concrete example removes ambiguity about exactly what the described formatting rule means in practice, similar to how examples help with style-matching more generally

questions.explanation: Just as with style-matching, a concrete formatting example resolves ambiguity that a purely verbal description might leave open.

questions.stem: A user finds that a specific request in a conversation and a Project's standing instruction give genuinely opposite guidance on an important point (not just a minor style preference). What is the most careful approach?

options.text: Assume one instruction is automatically and always correct with no further thought
Ignore both instructions and proceed with neither
Pause to explicitly clarify which should apply in this case, since a genuine substantive conflict (not just style) deserves deliberate resolution rather than a default assumption
Delete the Project immediately without resolving the specific conflict

questions.explanation: A substantive conflict — as opposed to a minor style question — deserves explicit clarification rather than an unexamined default assumption.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to prevent conflicting instructions from arising in the first place, rather than only resolving them after the fact?

options.text: Add new instructions freely with no consideration of how they interact with existing ones
Prevention is unnecessary since conflicts never actually cause any real issues
Before adding a new standing instruction, briefly check it against existing ones for potential contradiction
Conflicting instructions can never be prevented under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A brief consistency check before adding new standing instructions is a practical way to prevent conflicts from accumulating in the first place.

questions.stem: A user runs the same moderately complex task on two different tiers and finds the faster tier's output is indistinguishable in quality for their purposes. What is a reasonable conclusion?

options.text: The faster tier is likely a suitable, more cost-effective choice for this specific task going forward
The comparison is meaningless and should be ignored
The slower, more expensive tier should always be used regardless of this finding
Quality can never actually be compared across tiers

questions.explanation: An empirical head-to-head comparison showing equivalent quality is exactly the evidence needed to justify standardizing on the more cost-effective tier for that task.

questions.stem: What is a sound way to think about the relationship between Projects and Artifacts as product surfaces?

options.text: Artifacts always replace the need for Projects entirely
They are mutually exclusive and can never be used for related work
A Project can provide the persistent context for an ongoing body of work, within which individual Artifacts can hold specific substantial deliverables produced along the way
Projects always replace the need for Artifacts entirely

questions.explanation: Projects and Artifacts serve complementary roles — persistent context versus specific standalone deliverables — and are often used together.

questions.stem: A user is uncertain whether a task needs a research/search-enabled mode. What is a reasonable test question?

options.text: Does the request contain the word 'the'?
Is the task written in complete sentences?
Is the request longer than one paragraph?
Does the task depend on any fact that could have changed recently, or that requires up-to-the-moment information?

questions.explanation: Whether the task genuinely depends on current or recently-changing information is the substantive test for needing a search-enabled mode.

questions.stem: Why might a growing business periodically revisit its choice of Claude plan/deployment rather than treating the initial choice as permanent?

options.text: Plan choice should never be revisited once made
As team size, collaboration needs, and governance requirements evolve, a previously suitable plan may no longer be the best fit, warranting periodic reassessment
Revisiting plan choice always causes disruption with no benefit
Plan/deployment choice has no relationship to a business's evolving needs

questions.explanation: Evolving organizational needs are a legitimate reason to periodically reassess whether the current plan/deployment still fits, rather than treating the initial choice as permanent.

questions.stem: A Project is used by multiple people who each have slightly different preferences for a minor stylistic detail. How should this generally be handled?

options.text: Every individual preference must be permanently encoded into the standing Project instructions with no exceptions
Shared Projects can never accommodate any individual variation
Standing instructions should be left blank whenever more than one person uses a Project
The Project's standing instructions should capture the shared, agreed-upon baseline, with individuals able to state specific personal preferences within their own individual conversations as needed

questions.explanation: A shared baseline at the Project level, with room for individual, conversation-specific adjustments, reasonably balances consistency and personal preference.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable check to include when reviewing a Project's custom instructions for quality?

options.text: Whether the instructions are written in the longest possible sentences
Whether the instructions include as many unrelated topics as possible
Whether each instruction is clear, specific, and actually reflects a genuine standing need rather than a one-off preference
Whether the instructions avoid mentioning tone or format entirely

questions.explanation: Clarity, specificity, and genuine standing relevance are the practical quality markers for custom instructions, mirroring good prompt-writing principles.

questions.stem: A Project's knowledge sources have grown over time to include many documents, some no longer relevant to current work. What is a reasonable maintenance step?

options.text: Delete the entire Project rather than reviewing individual sources
Add even more unrelated documents to compensate for the growth
Periodically review the knowledge sources and remove or archive ones that are no longer relevant to the Project's current purpose
Never review or remove any knowledge source once added, regardless of continued relevance

questions.explanation: Periodic pruning of outdated or irrelevant knowledge sources keeps a Project's grounding material relevant and focused over time.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to consider the format and clarity of a document before adding it as a knowledge source, not just its topical relevance?

options.text: A topically relevant but poorly organized or unclear document may be harder to draw accurate, well-grounded information from than a clearer one
Clarity only matters for documents that will never actually be referenced
Only the file size of a document matters for its usefulness as a knowledge source
Format and clarity never affect how useful a knowledge source actually is

questions.explanation: Clarity and organization affect how reliably relevant information can actually be drawn from a document, not just whether the topic is a match.

questions.stem: A user wants to understand why a particular formatting preference applied in one conversation but not in a different, seemingly similar one within the same Project. What is a likely explanation to check first?

options.text: This kind of inconsistency is unexplainable and cannot be investigated
All conversations within the same Project are always identical in every respect
Projects apply instructions completely randomly with no discoverable pattern
The preference was likely stated as a one-off request in the first conversation rather than saved as a Project-level instruction, so it didn't carry over automatically

questions.explanation: Checking whether the preference was a one-off in-conversation request (versus a persisted Project-level instruction) is the most likely, checkable explanation.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable general rule of thumb for the scope of an instruction relative to how often it should apply?

options.text: Scope has no bearing on where an instruction should reasonably be placed
All instructions should always be placed at the Project level regardless of how narrowly they apply
Instructions meant to apply broadly and consistently belong at the Project level; instructions relevant to only a single specific request belong in that individual conversation
All instructions should always be placed within individual conversations regardless of how broadly they apply

questions.explanation: Matching instruction placement to its intended breadth of application — broad and recurring at the Project level, narrow and one-off within a conversation — is the sound rule of thumb.

questions.stem: A company is deciding between one large Project per department versus many small Projects per individual initiative. What is a reasonable factor in this decision?

options.text: Larger Projects are always better regardless of how distinct the underlying initiatives are
This decision should be made with no consideration of actual context overlap
The number of letters in the department's name
Whether initiatives within a department share enough common context/instructions to benefit from being grouped together, versus being distinct enough to warrant separate configuration

questions.explanation: The degree of genuine shared context between initiatives is the substantive factor in deciding Project granularity, not arbitrary factors like naming.

questions.stem: Why might overly fragmented Projects (many very narrow, single-purpose Projects with heavy overlap) create their own inefficiency?

options.text: Fragmentation never creates any inefficiency regardless of degree
Excessive fragmentation can lead to duplicated configuration effort and confusion about which nearly-identical Project to use for a given task
More Projects always means better organization with no downside
Fragmentation is only a concern for very small organizations

questions.explanation: Excessive fragmentation trades one problem (an overly broad Project) for another (duplicated setup and confusion among many overlapping narrow ones).

questions.stem: A team wants to standardize how new Projects are set up going forward (e.g., a checklist for instructions and knowledge sources to consider). What is the benefit of this practice?

options.text: Standardization always makes Project setup worse
No benefit; every new Project should be configured with no reference to prior practice
This practice is only relevant for organizations with a single Project
A standard setup checklist helps ensure new Projects are configured thoughtfully and consistently, reducing the chance of missing important context or knowledge sources

questions.explanation: A consistent setup checklist reduces the chance of overlooking important configuration and promotes consistency across a team's Projects.

questions.stem: A recurring low-stakes task occasionally surfaces genuinely high-stakes edge cases mixed in with routine ones. What is a reasonable design for handling this?

options.text: Escalate every single instance, including the routine ones, with no differentiation
Ignore the existence of high-stakes edge cases entirely since they're infrequent
Treat every instance identically as low-stakes with no differentiation
Build in a way to identify and flag the high-stakes edge cases specifically for escalation, while continuing to handle the genuinely routine cases with lighter-touch review

questions.explanation: Differentiating and specifically flagging the high-stakes edge cases for escalation — while keeping routine handling lightweight — is a proportionate design.

questions.stem: A piece of content is low-risk in isolation but will be combined with several other pieces into a single high-stakes public report. How should the individual piece be treated?

options.text: Combined use never changes the appropriate risk treatment of an individual component
It should always be treated as low-risk regardless of how it will ultimately be used
Only the final combined report needs any review; individual components never do
Its treatment should reflect the risk of its ultimate combined use in the high-stakes report, warranting more careful review than its standalone content might otherwise suggest

questions.explanation: Risk categorization should account for a component's ultimate use — a low-risk-seeming piece feeding into a high-stakes final product warrants review calibrated to that eventual use.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable approach when an organization's AI policy hasn't yet been updated to address a genuinely new type of use case?

options.text: Assume policies never need to be updated once written
Avoid ever raising the gap with anyone
Treat the gap as a prompt to seek guidance from an appropriate internal contact, and suggest the policy be updated to explicitly address the new use case going forward
Assume the new use case is automatically approved since it isn't explicitly addressed

questions.explanation: Proactively seeking guidance and flagging the policy gap is more responsible than assuming automatic approval for an unaddressed new use case.

questions.stem: A recurring monthly report reliably runs long enough to risk truncation. What is a durable process fix?

options.text: Continue generating it as one large request every month and manually asking to continue each time with no planning
Stop producing the monthly report altogether
Build the report generation process around a planned, sectioned approach from the start, given the known, predictable length
Randomly shorten the report's actual content every month with no relation to its real scope

questions.explanation: Since the length pattern is known and predictable for this recurring report, planning a sectioned approach from the outset is more durable than repeatedly reacting after each truncation.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable way to estimate whether a requested deliverable is at meaningful risk of truncation before starting?

options.text: Consider the scope and detail level requested (e.g., number of sections, depth of detail) relative to what similar past requests have needed, and section the work proactively if the scope looks large
Assume every request, regardless of scope, carries identical truncation risk
Only requests containing images ever carry truncation risk
Length risk can never be reasonably estimated in advance

questions.explanation: Comparing the requested scope/detail against what similar past requests have needed is a practical way to anticipate and proactively manage truncation risk.

questions.stem: A user repeatedly needs to analyze similarly-structured large documents (e.g., monthly reports of a consistent format). What is an efficient chunking approach?

options.text: Chunk each document into a random number of arbitrarily-sized pieces every time
Re-derive a completely new, ad hoc chunking strategy from scratch every single time with no reuse of past approach
Develop a consistent chunking approach based on the documents' shared, predictable structure, and reuse that approach each time this type of document needs processing
Avoid chunking these documents under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A reusable, structure-aware chunking approach is more efficient for recurring, similarly-structured documents than reinventing the strategy each time.

questions.stem: Why might chunking strategy need to differ between a document with clear section headers versus one that is one long undifferentiated block of text?

options.text: Chunking strategy should always be identical regardless of a document's internal structure
A document with clear headers offers natural, meaningful split points, while an undifferentiated block requires more careful judgment to find reasonable break points that preserve coherent meaning
Undifferentiated documents can never be chunked under any approach
Documents with headers should never be chunked at all

questions.explanation: The presence or absence of natural structural markers directly affects how straightforward it is to find coherent, meaning-preserving chunk boundaries.

questions.stem: A user wants variety across a batch of similar short pieces of content (e.g., ten product taglines) generated in a single request. What is a useful technique?

options.text: Provide no guidance at all and hope for natural variation across all ten
Request all ten with completely identical instructions and no differentiation between them
Explicitly assign a different constraint, angle, or tone to each of the ten within the same request, so each one is prompted toward a genuinely different result
Request only one tagline and duplicate it ten times

questions.explanation: Explicitly differentiating the angle or constraint for each item within a single batch request is a direct way to engineer genuine variety across the set.

questions.stem: What is a limitation of relying purely on asking for 'more creativity' to fix repetitive output, without any more specific guidance?

options.text: This approach always works perfectly with no limitation
Asking for creativity is the only approach that could ever work
A vague request for 'more creativity' gives no concrete direction, and may not reliably break a specific recurring pattern the way a more targeted change (persona, angle, explicit constraint) would
This limitation applies only to numerical content

questions.explanation: Vague requests for 'more creativity' lack the concrete, actionable specificity that a targeted change in framing or constraint provides.

questions.stem: A response uses inconsistent heading levels (e.g., jumping from a top-level heading directly to a deeply nested one with no intermediate levels). What is the appropriate fix?

options.text: Assume heading hierarchy can never be corrected
Accept the inconsistent heading structure since the content itself is accurate
Ask for the heading hierarchy to be corrected to a consistent, logical structure with appropriate intermediate levels
Remove all headings from the document entirely

questions.explanation: A direct request to fix the heading hierarchy into a logical, consistent structure is the straightforward fix for this kind of formatting problem.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to check formatting against the actual destination (e.g., a specific document template or platform) rather than judging it in isolation?

options.text: Formatting that looks fine in isolation may still not match the specific conventions or constraints of where it will actually be used, so checking against the real destination catches mismatches isolated review would miss
Destination-specific formatting requirements never matter
This consideration is only relevant for coding-related content
All destinations always accept identical formatting with no meaningful differences

questions.explanation: Destination-specific conventions can differ from generic 'good formatting,' so checking against the actual target catches mismatches that isolated review wouldn't surface.

questions.stem: A newly added Project instruction unintentionally contradicts a long-standing one that most users still expect to be in effect. What is a reasonable way to handle the transition?

options.text: Make the change silently with no communication to Project users
Communicate the change clearly to people who use the Project, and consider explicitly removing or updating the outdated instruction rather than leaving both in an unresolved contradictory state
Leave both contradictory instructions in place indefinitely with no communication
Delete the entire Project rather than resolving the specific contradiction

questions.explanation: Clear communication plus explicit resolution of the outdated instruction addresses both the practical contradiction and the risk of confusing existing users.

questions.stem: A user is midway through a very long generated list when it cuts off. Before asking Claude to continue, what is a useful quick check?

options.text: Note exactly where the content stopped, so the continuation can be checked for a clean, non-duplicated pickup at that precise point
There is no need to note where it stopped; continuations are always seamless with no verification needed
Assume the entire list must be regenerated from the very beginning
Assume the cutoff means the topic cannot be discussed further

questions.explanation: Noting the exact stopping point makes it easy to verify the continuation picks up cleanly, without gaps or duplication at the seam.

questions.stem: Which best summarizes a sound overall approach to conflicting instructions across scopes (Project-level vs. conversation-specific)?

options.text: Always assume conflicts are impossible and never check for them
Always delete all instructions at every level whenever any conflict is noticed
Notice the conflict, resolve it deliberately for the case at hand, and update the standing configuration if the conflict reveals the default itself needs to change
Always let the most recently typed instruction silently override everything with no further thought

questions.explanation: Deliberate noticing, resolving, and — where warranted — updating the standing default is the sound general pattern for handling instruction conflicts across scopes.
